Indic-Vedic—
Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra
Attention: This is a special edition of the *Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra* for the internet. When quoting, please indicate the editor and the date of the latest revision.

The *Vāsiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra*, edited by Harry Falk, Berlin, 1996: this text generally reproduces the reading of Alois Führer’s edition and has not been completely re-examined for errors of all kinds. A new edition based on a broad manuscript basis is nearing completion; its text differs significantly from that of this first submission.

The comparison with citations in the commentarial literature has yielded several lost textual fragments that are not included here. Inquiries regarding specific passages were made to Harry Falk. Upon completion of the edition, this entry will be replaced by the text of the critical edition. Conventions:
A hyphen “–” separates the members of compounds; an underscore “_” resolves sandhi within a sentence; two underscores followed by an apostrophe “__'” replace the *avagraha*.
Creation of the *ṭīṭūṣ*-version: Jost Gippert, Frankfurt am Main, June 1, 1996.
1. Now begins the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Dharma for the sake of the supreme good of man. 1.1. 2. And one who, having known it, practices it, is a righteous person (dhārmika). 1.2.
3. He becomes most praiseworthy in this world and, after death, attains the heavenly world.
1,3. 4. Dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti. 1,4. 5. In the absence of that, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas) is the authority. 1,5.

6. Furthermore, the cultured man (*śiṣṭa*) is one whose nature is free from desire. 1,6. 7. Dharma is that for which no [other] cause can be apprehended. 1,7. 8. Āryāvarta is the region east of the Adarśa mountains, west of the Kālaka forest, north of the Pāriyātra mountains, and south of the Himavat. 1,8.
9. And [the region] to the north of the Vindhya mountains. 1,9. 10. Whatever duties and whatever customs exist in that region are to be accepted everywhere. 1,10.
But not others, such as the duties of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma). 1,11.
<1> 12. Some say that [the land] between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers [is the land of Brahmanical luster].
13. Others say that as far as the black antelope roams, so far extends the land of Brahmanical luster.
14. Now, moreover, the Bhāllavins cite this verse in their *Nidāna*:
15. "In the west is the Sindhu, the restrainer; in the east is the rising of the sun."
"As long as Kṛṣṇa runs, so long indeed is there the splendor of Brahman. 1,15.
16. "That which those aged in the three Vedas should declare—"
People who know the Dharma [say] that the Dharma is found in both the sacred texts and in purification; there is no doubt about this. (1.16)
17. On account of the absence of revealed scripture (*śruti*), Manu has not declared the duties of regions, the duties of castes, and the duties of families. 1,17. 18.

One who goes forth before his elder brother, one who marries after his younger brother, one whose younger brother marries before him, one who marries before his elder sister who is marriageable, the husband of such a woman, a slayer of a hero, and a renouncer of the Veda—these are the sinners.
1,18. 19. They declare these [along with the aforementioned] to be the five great crimes (*mahāpātaka*). 1,19.

20. Violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, causing an abortion, stealing a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, and associating with outcasts [are the great sins]. 1.20. 21. Or [associating] through the Vedic lineage or through marriage. 1.21.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year, whether through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or gifts. (1.22)

23. One who casts away the sacred fires, one who strikes back at his teacher, an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, and one who sells *soma*—these are minor offenses (*upapātaka*). 1.23. 24. A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives in the order of the castes; a Kṣatriya two; and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra each one. 1.24. 25. Some say that a Brāhmaṇa may also take a Śūdra wife, provided he excludes her from the *mantras*, just like the others. 1.25.
26. One should not act in such a manner. 1.26. 27. For from this follows the certain ruin of the family and the loss of heaven after death. 1.27. 28. There are six types of marriage. 1.28.
29. [The forms of marriage are] the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Gāndharva, the Kṣātra, and the Mānuṣa.
1,29. 30. That which one should give with water preceded by a request is the Brāhma.
1,30. 31. When the sacrificial ritual has been spread out, giving a daughter to the officiating priest while he is performing his duty after having adorned her, that they call the Daiva. 1,31.

32. And that which is performed with a pair of cattle is the Ārṣa. 1,32. 33. When one desires a willing woman of equal birth and marries her, that is the Gāndharva. 1,33. 34. That which they carry off by force, having violently overpowered her, is the Kṣātra. 1,34.

35. Having made a bargain, that man has purchased her with wealth. 1,35. 36. Therefore, for one who possesses a daughter, a hundred [cows] plus a chariot should be given; thus is the purchase understood here. 1,36. <3>
37. "She who, having been purchased by her husband, then acts with others"—this is stated in the Cāturmāsya [sacrifices].
38. Furthermore, they also cite:
"Lost knowledge returns once again."
But with the destruction of the family, there is the destruction of everything in this world;
for even a horse is honored by means of its lineage, and therefore they marry women of noble birth. (1.38)
39. The three social classes shall live according to the instruction of the Brāhmaṇa. 40. The Brāhmaṇa shall proclaim the duties (dharma). 41. And the king shall enforce them.

42. But the king, ruling according to dharma, shall take a sixth part of the wealth [of his subjects]. 1.42. 43. Except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa. 1.43. 44. For it is said that he partakes of a sixth share of the merit derived from sacrifices and charitable works. 1.44.

45. A Brāhmaṇa makes the Veda abundant; a Brāhmaṇa rescues one from calamity. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten [as food]; Soma is his king—so it is said. 1.45. 46. And it is known from tradition that there is prosperity after death—so it is known, so it is known.
1.46. Thus ends the first chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. 1.1.
There are four castes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
(2,1) Three castes are twice-born: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya. (2,2) Of these... (2,3)
The first birth is from the mother; the second is at the binding of the girdle of muñja grass.
Here, his mother is said to be the Sāvitrī, and the teacher is called the father.
(2.3) They call the teacher "father" because of his bestowing of the Veda. (2.4)
Nevertheless, they cite this:
"Indeed, there are two kinds of seed for a man;
for a Brahmin, one is above the navel and the other is below it."
Now, that which is above the navel—by means of that he procreates offspring when he initiates Brahmins, when he teaches them, when he performs sacrifices for them, and when he does what is good.

But that which is below the navel—by means of that his offspring is born here in this world. Therefore, they do not say of one who is learned in the Vedas and has studied them thoroughly, "You are childless.
Thus says Hārīta as well.
For no ritual action whatsoever exists for him prior to the tying of the girdle of munja grass;
indeed, in terms of livelihood, he is equal to a Śūdra.
"Until he is born in the Veda," 2.6.7.
"Except for acts involving water, the *svadhā* offering, and those connected with the ancestors," 2.6.8.
"Knowledge, indeed, came to the Brahmin. 2.6.9.
Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who lacks self-control; thus shall I be full of power. 2.8.
<5> 9. Only to one whom you know to be pure, vigilant, wise, and endowed with the practice of celibacy, [should you impart this].
O Brahmin, speak to him who would not deceive you in any way, who is a guardian of the treasure,
One who brings about freedom from suffering and bestows the deathless—him one should regard as both father and mother; one should not harbor any ill will whatsoever toward him. (2.10)
Those Brahmins who, having been taught, do not honor their teacher in word, thought, or deed, are just as those by whom the teacher should not be fed.
In the same way, that sacred learning does not benefit them.
Just as fire burns dry grass, so does the Veda, when questioned but treated with disrespect, burn the one who asks it.
"One should not proclaim the Veda to him who does not show honor. (2.12) "There are six duties for a Brāhmaṇa. (2.13)
14. For the Brāhmaṇa, [the duties are]: studying one's own Veda, teaching it, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
2.14. 15. Three [of these] apply to the Rājanya (Kṣatriya). 2.15. 16. Namely: studying, sacrificing for oneself, and giving gifts. 2.16.
17. Protecting the subjects by means of weapons is his own duty; he should live by that. 2,17. 18. These same [duties] belong to the Vaiśya. 2,18.
19. Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending [are the occupations of the Vaiśya].
2,19. 20. Service to these [higher castes] is the fixed duty and livelihood of the Śūdra.
2,20. 21. All [the twice-born] shall have their hair and dress regulated; or they may all have their hair loose, except for the topknot. 2,21.
22. Those who cannot subsist by their own duty should adopt the next lower mode of life.
2,22. 23. But never the higher one.
2,23. 24. Having adopted the livelihood of a Vaiśya, those living by trade [should avoid the following]: [text continues]

Stones, salt, gems, whetstones, silk, linen, and skins; 2,24. 25. And all woven cloth that is dyed red; 2,25. 26. Prepared food, flowers, fruits, roots, perfumes, flavors, water, the juice of medicinal plants, Soma, weapons, poison, meat, milk and its derivatives, iron, tin, lac, lead, and 2,26.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt; by selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days. (2.27)
28. Among village animals, those with solid hoofs and those with manes, as well as all wild animals, birds, and fanged beasts [are not to be eaten].
2,28. 29. Regarding grains, they say that sesame seeds [are the most important]. 2,29. 30. Now, moreover, they cite this:
If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or as an ointment, one becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with one's ancestors. (2.30) <7>
31. Or, at their own will, they may cultivate sesame themselves and sell it.
32. Therefore, he should be a ploughman before his morning meal, using two bulls that have testicles, are not castrated, and have not been yoked previously.
33. In the summer, one should give water. 2,33. 34.
"The plough, tipped with iron, well-guided, with its handle for the sake of Soma—that ploughs up the cow, the sheep, and the fat, swelling female; it provides a wagon for the chariot. 2,34.

35. "The plough, with its keen share, accompanied by heroes, by good men, and by oxen—auspicious, with a beautiful nose, for its nose is indeed auspicious; it sows by means of the nose. With a handle that reaches the Soma, for the Soma reaches its handle—it sows: cattle and sheep, goats, horses, mules, and camels; and a cow that is well-fed, beautiful, auspicious, and a young maiden for the first time.
(2,35) 36. "For how indeed could one plough with a plough except for the sale of grain? (2,36)
37. Flavors may be bartered for flavors, whether they are superior or inferior.
2,37. 38. But salt must never be bartered for other flavors. 2,38. 39. Sesame, rice, cooked food, and human beings are prescribed as items for exchange. 2,39.
40. A Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya shall not pay interest on a loan. 2,40. 41. Now they also quote:
"Having taken grain at the current market price..."
He who bestows that which is of great value is indeed called a usurer, and is censured among those who discourse on Brahman. 2.41.
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against an increase [in merit] on a scale; the killer of an embryo remained outweighed by ten million [of the latter].
"The usurer trembled.
(2,42) Or they may give it to one who has abandoned his duties or to a drunkard. (2,43)
44. Gold is [to be repaid] twofold, and grain threefold. 2.44. 45. Liquids are explained by the same rule as grain. 2.45. 46. So too are flowers, roots, and fruits. 2.46.
47. Eightfold [interest] on gold weighed by scales. 2,47. 48. Moreover, they also cite:
two, three, and four [percent].
And five percent per month is prescribed as the interest to be taken from the social classes in their respective order. (2.48)
But the king, by means of the state of death, may destroy the increase of wealth; then, by means of the royal consecration, he may restore it.
And the principal substance increases. (2,49) Now hear the rate of interest proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha regarding usury. (2,50)
"Five māṣas for twenty [paṇas];
thus the law is not violated. (2.50) "It is not violated. (2.51)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||2||
3.1 Those who are not learned in the Vedas, who do not recite the invitatory verses, or who do not maintain the sacred fires, become equal in status to Śūdras.
In this regard, they cite this verse of Manu:
The twice-born who, without having studied the Veda,
exerts himself in other matters, becomes a Śūdra even while still alive.
He goes swiftly along with his lineage.
3,2.3 A Brāhmaṇa does not become one who is not a reciter of the Ṛgveda, nor a merchant, nor an actor.
He who does not carry out the commands of a Śūdra, nor is a thief, nor a physician; 3,3.
The king should punish that village where twice-born men live without observing vows, do not study the Vedas, and subsist on forbidden food.
For he is indeed the provider of food for thieves.
3.4.5 To those who observe no vows, who possess no sacred mantras, and who subsist merely by their caste—
Among those gathered by the thousands,
there is no true assembly when those who speak are deluded by darkness. 3.5.6
Fools do not understand the Dharma; that evil, becoming a hundredfold, falls upon those who preach it. (3.6)
Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas may declare,
that should be known as Dharma.
Not for others by the thousands;
3.7.8 sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya) should always be given to one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
For what is given to one who is not learned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities;
likewise for him in whose single household there is a fool.
Even if he is far away, one who is learned in the scriptures is worthy of gifts; one should give to the learned, for there is no transgression in doing so. 3.9.
There is no bypassing of a Brahmin who is devoid of the Vedas; it would be like abandoning a blazing fire.
For indeed, no offering is poured into ashes. 3,10 | 11.
And that which is an elephant made of wood, and that which is a deer made of leather—
And a Brahmin who does not study—these three are merely bearers of names.
(3.11) Those who are ignorant eat the food of the learned. (3.12)
In whichever kingdoms they eat, those lands suffer from drought or a great danger arises. (3.12)
13. Whatever property a king may discover that has been unclaimed, he shall take it after giving a sixth part to the finder. 3.13. 14.
But if a Brāhmaṇa who is engaged in the six duties should discover it, the king shall not take it. 3.14.
15. Having slain an *ātatāyin* (an assailant), they say there is no sin whatsoever for the one who takes his life. 3.15. 16. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"The incendiary and the poisoner..."
One with a weapon in hand, a robber of wealth, and likewise one who seizes land or a wife— these six are assassins (ātatāyin). 3.16.
One may slay even one who has mastered the Vedas if he approaches as an assassin intent on killing.
By that act, he does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
(3.17) 18 He who would slay an assailant born in a noble family and devoted to the study of the Vedas—
"By that [act], he would not be a killer of an embryo; rather, it is fury that meets fury. 3.18.
19. One who knows the three *Ākhyānas*, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the *Tri-suparṇa* hymn, one who knows the four *Medhas*, and a follower of the *Vājasaneyi*.

One who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*), one who maintains the lineage of a *brahmadeya* grant, a singer of the *Chāndogya*, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, and he who studies the Dharmas— those whose maternal and paternal lineages for ten generations are known to be learned *śrotriyas* and who are themselves learned *snātakas*— these are the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). 3.19.
One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the three principal orders of life— these are the chief ones.
Their assembly consists of at least ten members. 3,20.
Having initiated him and taught him the entire Veda, he is an Ācārya. 3,21.
22. But he who teaches even a single portion [of the Veda] is an *upādhyāya*. 3,22. 23. And so is one who teaches the *vedāṅgas*.
3,23. 24. For the sake of self-protection or when castes are intermingling, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms. 3,24.
25. But for a Kṣatriya, that [offering] is indeed constant, because of his duty to protect. 3,25. <11> 26. Having washed his feet and his hands...
Sitting to the east or north of the *maṇibandha* (the wrist), the line above the root of the thumb is the *brāhma* *tīrtha*; with it, one should sip water three times silently.
(3.26) One should wipe the mouth twice. (3.27) One should touch the cavities of the head with water. (3.28)

29. He should pour water on the crown of his head and on his left hand. 3,29. 30. One should not perform ācamana while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing. 3,30. 31. A Brāhmaṇa should do so with water that reaches the heart, which is free from bubbles and froth. 3,31.
32. A Kṣatriya [is purified] by [water] reaching the throat; 3,32. 33. A Vaiśya by water that has been sipped;
3,33. 34. And a woman or a Śūdra by water merely touched; 3,34.

35. Even from a fissure, those [waters] which are capable of sustaining cows [are pure]. 3,35. 36. Nor [are they pure] those that are corrupted by color, smell, or taste, nor those that flow toward impurity. 3,36.
37. Drops that do not touch the body do not make one impure by defilement.
38. Having slept, eaten, sneezed, drunk, wept, or bathed, and having sipped water, one should sip water again after putting on a garment.
39. One should also sip water after touching the lips where there is no hair.
40. There is no fault in [food] adhering to the beard.
3,40. 41. And that which may be stuck between the teeth, like [particles of] food between the teeth, [is not a fault].
If there should be a remnant after one has sipped water,
one becomes pure by simply swallowing it.
Even for one who is causing others to rinse their mouths,
those drops that have fallen do not cause impurity from remnants.
But those stages are known to be equal when one is engaged in the consumption of food.
<12> 43. While moving about in the acts of eating, etc., [one remains in equipoise].
If he should touch something defiled by food remnants, he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and proceed again. 3.43.
44. Whatever may require examination, one should touch it with water.
45. Wild animals killed by dogs, and fruit fallen from birds, [are pure].
That which is not frequented by fools,
that which is practiced by women, and that merchandise which is displayed for sale— (3.45–46)
And whatever defects exist in the faces of women,
he is not harmed by gadflies or flies that settle upon him. 3.46–47.
Having enumerated all those waters that abide upon the earth and those which provide nourishment for cows, [he should offer them].
"Prajāpati said that [the body] is pure," so it is stated in 3.47.
48. Purity consists in the removal of stains and odors from that which is smeared with impurities.

With water and earth. 3.48. 49. For objects made of metal, clay, wood, and woven fibers, the purifications are respectively: ash, wiping, burning, scraping, and washing. 3.49. 50. Stones and gems are purified like metal. 3.50.

51. [The purification] of gems, coral, conch-shells, and mother-of-pearl is like that of wood. 3,51. 52. [The purification] of bones is like that of wood. 3,52. 53. [The purification] of ropes, split bamboo, and leather is like that of cloth. 3,53.
54. [The purification] of vessels made of fruit is by means of cow-hair. 3.54. 55. [The purification] of those made of linen is by means of a paste of white mustard.
3.55. 56. But the earth attains purity through sweeping, smearing, scraping, sprinkling, and the application of implements, according to the specific defect and its location. 3.56.
<13> 58 A woman is purified by her menses; a river is purified by its current.
Bell-metal is purified by ashes; earthenware by re-firing; [and] that which has been defiled by liquors, urine, or excrement [is purified by scrubbing with cow-dung]. 3.58–59.
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with phlegm, pus, tears, or blood cannot be purified again by firing it. 3.59.
The limbs are purified by water;
the mind is purified by truth; and the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity.
"The intellect is purified by knowledge" (3.60). "Gold is purified by water alone" (3.61). "Likewise silver" (3.62).
63. Copper is purified by acid.
3.63. 64. At the base of the little finger is the *tīrtha* of the gods (*daiva*). 3.64. 65. On the tips of the fingers is that of the sages (*ṛṣi*). 3.65.

66. On the tips of the fingers is that of humans (mānuṣa). 3,66. 67. In the middle of the palm is that of Agni (āgneya). 3,67. 68. Between the forefinger and the thumb is that of the ancestors (pitrya). 3,68.

69. One should respond with "It is pleasing" when offered food in the morning or evening meals. 3,69. 70. One should respond with "It is well-prepared" at rites for the ancestors (śrāddha). 3,70. 71. One should respond with "It is excellent" at rites for prosperity; [this applies] repeatedly to all rites for prosperity. 3,71.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||3||
The fourfold caste system is distinguished by its origin and by specific sacramental rites. 4.1.14.1.
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya.
"A Śūdra was born from the feet"—thus also there is a Vedic verse (nigama).

From the Gāyatrī he created the Brāhmaṇa, from the Triṣṭubh the Rājanya, and from the Jagatī the Vaiśya; but [he did] not [create] the Śūdra by means of any metre. Thus he is known to be one who is not to be consecrated (asaṃskārya). 4,3.
4. Truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, non-violence, and procreation [are duties] for all.
5. "One may indeed kill an animal for the worship of ancestors, deities, and guests"—this is the teaching of Manu.
6. [This applies] at the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*) and at a sacrifice.
"In the rites for the ancestors and the gods,
one should indeed kill an animal here, and not otherwise," so Manu has declared. (4.6)
7. Indeed, meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings,
and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven.
Therefore, in a sacrifice, killing is not killing.
(4.7) Furthermore, if a bull or a large goat is cooked for a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya who has arrived as a guest, thinking, "In this way we are performing hospitality for him," [it is not killing].
(4.8) The water-libation rite and the period of impurity begin from the second year [of age]. (4.9)
10. Some say [the impurity lasts] until the eruption of teeth.
4,10. 11. Having consigned the body to the fire, they enter the water without looking back.
4,11. 12. They should perform the water-rites with both hands; on odd-numbered days, they should face the south. 4,12.
13. This southern quarter indeed belongs to the ancestors.
14. Having gone to their house, they should sit for three days upon a layer of grass (prastara) without eating.
15. In the event of inability [to maintain themselves], they should subsist on what has been purchased or produced [by others].
4.15. 16. Impurity (*āśauca*) due to death (*śāva*) is prescribed for ten days among *sapiṇḍas*.
4.16. 17. *Sapiṇḍa* status is understood to extend to the seventh person [in the lineage]. 4.17.

18. And for women who have been given away in marriage, the [lineage] is known to extend through three generations. 4.18. 19. For those who have been given away, the others (the paternal relatives) shall perform [the rites], and they (the maternal relatives) shall do so for them. 4.19. 20. The same rule applies even in the case of birth. 4.20.
For those who desire thorough purity: 4.20. Or [purity] regarding the mother and father: 4.21.
Some say it is [sufficient] regarding the mother alone, because she is the cause of that [birth]: 4.22.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth, provided he does not come into contact [with the woman]."

"In that case, the *rajas* (menstrual blood) is to be known as impure, and it does not exist in a male. (4.23) "If, however, it should enter again internally, they would be purified by the remainder [of the penance]. (4.24)
25. During the remainder of the night, [he should recite] two verses. 4,25. 26. At dawn, three verses. 4,26. 27. A Brāhmaṇa [is purified] in ten nights. 4,27.
28. A Kṣatriya [is purified] in fifteen nights. 4,28. 29. A Vaiśya [is purified] in twenty nights. 4,29. 30. A Śūdra becomes pure in one month. 4,30.
31. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who has eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or even during a birth-impurity (sūtaka),..."
He shall go to a terrible hell and be born among the animal wombs. 4,31.
If a twice-born man, having been appointed to officiate at a funeral rite, eats while the ten-day period of impurity has not yet passed,
he becomes a worm at the end of his body.
"He consumes that excrement," so it is said. (4.32) It is known from tradition that by studying the *Saṃhitā* while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months, one becomes purified.
(4.33) When a child dies who is less than two years old, or in the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts three nights. (4.34)

35. Gautama says that there is immediate purification (sadyaḥ-śauca). 4.35. 36. If a deceased person is staying in another country, one shall observe impurity for one night upon hearing of it after the ten days have passed. 4.36. 37. If one who has maintained the sacred fires dies while away from home, Gautama says that after performing the cremation rites again, the purification is the same as for a corpse. 4.37.

38. Having touched a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, a cremation ground, a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, or anything impure, one should enter the water with the head for purification—yes, into the water.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||4||
5.1 A woman is not independent; she has man as her primary authority.
5.2 It is known that [the offering] is "immortal" when it is without fire and when the woman is not in her courses.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth."
"And a son [is the authority] when she has reached old age;
for a woman does not deserve independence. 5.3.4. Her husband's [authority] is [the rule] in the event of misconduct.
The expiation for secret sins has been stated. (5.4) For month after month, their menstrual flow indeed washes away their misdeeds. (5.5)
6. A woman in her menses remains impure for three nights. 5,6. <17> 7. She must not apply ointments.
He should not anoint himself, he should not bathe in water, and he should sleep on the ground.
He should not sleep during the day, nor touch fire, nor let go of his rope.
He should not brush his teeth, nor eat meat,
nor gaze at the planets.
One should not laugh,
nor act in any way, nor run.
One should drink from a bowl that is not deformed, or one may drink from the hollow of the joined palms, or from a vessel made of red iron. 5.7.
For it is known:

after Indra had slain the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he was seized by evil and thought of himself, "I am bound by great unrighteousness. All beings reviled him, crying out, "Foe of the embryo! Foe of the embryo! He ran to women, saying, "Accept a third part of this murder of the embryo for me. They said, "What shall come to us? He replied, "Choose a boon."

They said, "Let us obtain offspring during the fertile season; let us unite according to our desire until the birth. "So be it," they agreed. Thus, this very sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) manifests month after month. Therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman in her courses; she stands there having assumed the form of the sin of killing an embryo. Regarding this, they say: "One must not accept ointment or oil for her, for that is the food of a woman. Therefore, people feel disgust toward her and toward that [food], thinking, "She has come near me. As for those whose wives remain in their courses...
And whoever are without sacred fires,
and those whose family is devoid of Vedic learning—
all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.
"All of them possess the characteristics of Śūdras.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
<18> 6.1 Conduct is the supreme dharma.
This is the certainty for all:
one whose soul is overwhelmed by base conduct perishes both in this world and after death. 6.1.
Neither austerities, nor sacred knowledge, nor the Agnihotra sacrifice, nor sacrificial fees can save this man who has fallen away from this [path] due to his deficient conduct.
They do not rescue one by any means.
6.2.3: The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences.
At the time of death, desires abandon him, just as birds with grown wings leave their nest. (6.3) But for a Brahmin who is devoid of proper conduct...
The Vedas in their entirety, along with their six auxiliary limbs and the sacrifices, are capable of producing what joy for the blind man, appearing like beautiful women? 6.4.
The Vedic meters do not deliver this deceitful person from his wickedness when he persists in deceit,
even though both syllables are being studied correctly.
That sacred knowledge (brahman) purifies him, just as the rains purify the fields. 6,5.
6. For a man of evil conduct indeed becomes censured in the world.
One who constantly shares in suffering is diseased and short-lived. (6,6) Dharma bears fruit through right conduct. (7)
From good conduct one obtains wealth;
from good conduct one attains prosperity; good conduct destroys inauspicious marks. 6.7.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks,
the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from malice—
He lives for a hundred years. 6,8.
<19> 9. The applications of eating, excretion, and movement.
One who knows the Dharma should keep [the senses] well-restrained;
likewise, speech, intellect, vigor, austerity, wealth, and life itself must be kept most carefully guarded. (6.9)
10. One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day, but at night one should do so facing south.
In this way, indeed, one's life-span is not diminished. 6,10.
11 Facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, and facing a twice-born man, [one should study].
If one urinates toward the sun, water, or during the twilight, wisdom perishes;
one should not urinate in a river. 6.11–12.
Not on a path, nor on ashes, nor on cow dung, nor on ploughed land, nor on sown ground, nor in the shade of trees that provide livelihood for grass-eating animals. 6.12.
In shade or in darkness,
by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the ritual] facing whichever direction is comfortable for him.

And in cases of danger to life or fear [of death], one may perform [purificatory acts] with water drawn up from a source. (6.14) One should perform [other rites] with water that has been drawn up; however, bathing may be done even with water that has not been drawn up. (6.15)
16. A Brahmin should likewise fetch earth from a riverbank containing sand. 17. [He should also take it] from within the water or from a temple.
The five types of earth that should not be taken are: from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, or that which remains after purification has been performed. 6.17.
One application of clay on the penis, three on the hands, two on both [hands together],
five on the anus, and ten on each [of the other two feet].
For both, there are seven applications of clay. (6.18) 19. This is the purification for a householder; it is double for a student.
For the forest-dweller it is threefold, but for ascetics it is fourfold. 6.19.
The meal of a sage consists of eight mouthfuls,
that of a forest-dweller sixteen,
and that of a householder thirty-two.
The life of a celibate student is immeasurable. 6,20.
21. These three—the ox, the celibate student, and the one who has maintained the sacred fires—are [inexhaustible].
Only those who eat attain success; for them there is no success while fasting. [This applies] to the taking away of asceticism and gifts. 6.21–22.
He who is not the eldest in vows, observances, sacrifices, study, and duties— he is not our third. 6.22.
Yoga, austerity, self-control, charity,
truthfulness, purity, compassion, sacred learning, knowledge, realization, and faith.
This is the characteristic of a Brahmin:
those who are peaceful and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with the Vedas, who have conquered their senses, and who abstain from killing living beings.
Those Brahmins whose hands shrink back when receiving gifts are capable of delivering [others]. 6.25. 25a.
And one who is envious and a slanderer...
The ungrateful, the long-simmering with anger—these four are outcastes by their actions; the fifth is the outcaste by birth. 6.25a.
Long-standing enmity, envy, untruthfulness, reviling the Vedas, backbiting,
and cruelty.
One should know the characteristics of a Śūdra. 6.24. 26. One vessel consists of the Veda; another vessel consists of austerity.
Even among vessels, that vessel is the true vessel whose belly does not contain the food of a Śūdra.
(6.26) One whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food... (28)
Even though he constantly studies, and even though he offers oblations and performs sacrifices, he does not find the higher goal. 6,28.
Any twice-born man who dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach shall become a village pig.
Or it arises in his family:
"But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra [is born as such]. (6.27.29)
The sons belong to him whose food they eat;
he shall not ascend to heaven. 6,29.
One who has arisen from Vedic study, possesses a noble lineage, is tranquil,
established in the sacrificial rites, fearful of sin, possessed of great knowledge, patient toward women, righteous, and a protector of cows— [such a person should be honored].
They say such a person, exhausted by vows, is a worthy recipient (pātra). 6,30.
Just as milk, curd, ghee, or honey placed in an unbaked clay vessel [perishes], 31.
It would be ruined through the weakness of the vessel; and so too would that vessel and those essences. 6.31–32. Likewise with cattle and gold.
An ignorant person who accepts clothing, a horse, land, or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes like wood. 6.32.
33. One should not play with one's limbs or fingernails as musical instruments. 6,33. 34. Nor [should one do so] with the fingernails at the beginning of a meal or other such occasions. 6,34. 35.
Nor should one drink water with cupped hands (añjali). 6,35.
36. One should not strike water with the foot or with the hand. 37. Nor should one strike water with water.
38. One should not pluck fruits with bricks. 6.38. 39. Nor should one pluck one fruit with another fruit. 6.39. 40.
One should not be deceitful nor fraudulent. 6.40.
41. One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas. 6.41. 42. Furthermore, they cite this example:
one should not be fickle with hands or feet.
One should not be fickle with the eyes, nor fickle with speech or limbs; such is the sphere of activity for the disciplined. 6.42.
Those for whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been handed down through traditional succession, [are the authorities].
Those Brahmins who have the Vedas as their direct authority should be known as the learned; [they are those] for whom one is neither existent nor non-existent. 6.43.
He who knows neither the unlearned nor the learned,
neither the well-conducted nor the ill-conducted,
he is a Brāhmaṇa.
"He is a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||6||
7.1 There are four stages of life (āśramas): 7.2 the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka).

3. Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, he who has maintained his vow of studentship may live with whomever he wishes. 7.3. 4. A student shall serve his teacher until the liberation from the body [i.e., death]. 7.4. 5. And when the teacher has died, he shall serve the sacred fire. 7.5.
For it is known that Agni is your teacher (7.6).
He should be restrained in speech (7.7). He should eat at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times (7.8).
9. He should practice begging for alms. 7.9. 10. He should remain dependent on his teacher. 7.10. 11.
He should wear his hair matted, or have a single lock of hair matted. 7.11.

12. He should follow the teacher when he is walking; if [the teacher] is sitting, he should stand; if [he] is lying down, he should sit beside him. 7,12. 13. He should study when called upon. 7,13. 14. Having offered everything he has obtained, he should eat with his permission. 7,14.
15. He shall avoid [using] a bed, a couch, tooth-cleansing wood, washing, collyrium, ointment, shoes, and an umbrella. 7,15.
16. He shall stand during the day and sit at night. 7,16.
17. "One should approach water three times a day, saying, 'Water! Water!
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||7||

8.1 A householder, having subdued anger and joy and being permitted by his teacher, shall bathe and take a wife who is of the same *ṛṣi* lineage, who has not had sexual intercourse, who is younger in age, and of equal status.
8.2 [She should be] fifth [removed] from her maternal relatives and seventh from her paternal relatives.
3. One should kindle the domestic fire for marriage ceremonies. 8.3. 4. One should not turn away a guest who has arrived in the evening.
8.4. 5. No one should dwell in his house without eating. 8.5.
If a Brahmin seeking lodging comes to one's house and does not eat,
whatever merit that person has earned shall belong to him.
Taking everything with him, he departs. (8.6) A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally considered a guest.
Since he stays for only a non-permanent duration,
he is therefore called a guest;
one who belongs to the same village is not a guest.
Likewise, a learned Brahmin who is a guest should not stay in someone's house without eating, whether the proper time has arrived or not. 8.8.

9. One who is faithful by nature and free from covetousness is fit for the establishment of the sacred fires; he should not fail to maintain the fires. 8.9. 10. And he is fit for the Soma sacrifice; he should not be one who does not offer the Soma. 8.10. 11.
He should be devoted to Vedic study, to sacrifice, and to procreation. 8.11.
12. One should honor a guest who has arrived at one's house by rising to meet him, offering a seat, speaking kind words, and being free from envy. 8.12.
And one should sustain all beings with food according to one's ability. 8.13.
14. It is the householder alone who sacrifices; the householder performs austerity; indeed, [he is the foremost] among the four stages of life.

And the householder is distinguished [as superior]. 8.14. 15 Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 16 As all the Vedas, together with their secret portions (rahasya), find their culmination in the Upanishads, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 17 As all living beings, moving and stationary, find their support in the earth, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 18 As all actions, whether performed by body, speech, or mind, find their completion in knowledge, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 19 As all sacrificial rites, including the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Cāturmāsya, and the Nirūḍhapaśubandha, find their fulfillment in the Agniṣṭoma, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 20 As the four kinds of living beings—those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born from sprouts—all find their sustenance in food, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 21 As all the worlds, beginning with that of the ancestors, find their support in the world of heaven, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 22 As all the Vedas, including the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda, find their culmination in the Upanishads, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 23 As all the sacrificial fires—the Gārhapatya, Āhavanīya, Dakṣiṇāgni, Sabhya, and Āvasathya—find their source in the Gārhapatya fire, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 24 As all the gods, beginning with Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Prajāpati, and Brahmā, find their origin in Prajāpati, so do all stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder. 8.15. 25 As all the stages of life find their fulfillment in the householder, so the householder who maintains his sacred fires and performs his duties is said to be equal to all the stages of life combined. 8.15. 26 As the householder supports his parents, his wife, his children, his servants, his guests, and his kin, he thereby supports the entire world. 8.15. 27 As the householder offers oblations to the gods, libations to the ancestors, and food to men, and as he protects all creatures, he is indeed the very foundation of the world. 8.15. 28 As the householder performs the five great sacrifices (mahāyajña) daily, he attains inexhaustible merit and secures the welfare of all beings. 8.15. 29 As the householder practices charity, self-restraint, truthfulness, compassion, and purity, he becomes worthy of honor in this world and the next. 8.15. 30 Thus, the householder is preeminent among all stages of life; he is the source of all, the support of all, and the means by which the eternal dharma is maintained. 8.15. 31 Therefore, one should strive to fulfill the duties of a householder with diligence, for therein lies the highest good and the path to liberation. 8.15. 32 As all rivers and streams flow into the ocean and remain there, so do all virtues and duties find their final rest in the householder. 8.15. 33 As the ocean receives all waters without being filled, so the householder receives all guests and offerings without being satiated. 8.15. 34 As the sun dispels darkness and brings light to the world, so the householder dispels the darkness of ignorance through his virtuous conduct. 8.15. 35 As the earth sustains all beings without discrimination, so the householder sustains all dependents with impartiality and kindness. 8.15. 36 Thus, the householder is the most excellent stage of life, for it is the foundation upon which the entire social order rests. 8.15. 37 One who fulfills these duties with devotion attains the highest state, transcending all worldly bonds and reaching the realm of the immortals. 8.15. 38 Therefore, let the householder be vigilant in his duties, for such a life is the true path to prosperity and ultimate liberation. 8.15. 39 As all rivers and streams find their ultimate stability in the ocean, so do all the stages of life find their final repose in the householder. 8.15. 40 Thus ends the discourse on the preeminence of the householder stage of life. 8.15. 41 May this teaching bring peace and prosperity to all beings. 8.15. 42 Let all follow this path with faith and devotion. 8.15. 43 Thus concludes the section on the
