In this way, all those belonging to the stages of life find their support in the householder, just as [all beings] depend upon the mother. 8.15–16.
All living beings live; even so, all mendicants live by depending upon the householder. 8,16.
One who constantly uses water for purification, always wears the sacred thread, constantly engages in Vedic study, avoids the food of outcasts,
approaches his wife during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules;
A Brahmin does not fall from the world of Brahmā—from the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||8||
9.1 The forest-dweller has matted hair and wears garments of bark or deerskin.
9.2 He shall not enter a village.
3. He shall not stand upon land that has been ploughed. 9,3. 4.
He shall gather roots and fruits from unploughed ground. 9,4. 5. He shall remain chaste (with his vital energy drawn upward). 9,5.
6. One whose disposition is forgiveness. 9,6. 7. One should honor a guest who has arrived at the hermitage with alms consisting of roots and fruits. 9,7. 8.
One should only give, and not accept [gifts]. 9,8.
9. He should perform the ritual touching of water at the three periods of the day. 9.9. 10. Having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, he should be one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
9.10. 11. Dwelling at the foot of a tree, after six months have passed, he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling. 9.11.
He who gives to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings shall go to eternal heaven; thus it is called "eternal. 9.12.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||9||
10.1 A wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), having given the gift of fearlessness to all living beings, may depart.
10.2 Now they also quote:
For that sage who wanders having granted fearlessness to all beings,
[there is likewise fearlessness] from all beings.
Fear never exists for him. 10.2.3 He who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from [taking their lives], possesses no fear.
Having accepted wealth, one destroys both those already born and those yet to be born; therefore, one should renounce all actions. 10.3.4.4.
One should not renounce the Veda;
by renouncing the Veda one becomes a Śūdra;
therefore, one should not renounce the Veda. 10.4.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman;
breath control is the supreme austerity; begging is superior to fasting.
Compassion is superior to giving. (10.5) Shaven-headed, free from the sense of "mine," and without possessions. (10.6) He should go for alms to seven houses that have not been pre-selected. (10.7)
8. When the smoke has ceased and the pestle has been laid aside. 10.8. 9. Wearing a single garment. 10.9.
10. Or, having covered his body with a deerskin or with grass cut from cow-paths; 11. He should sleep on the bare ground; 12.
He should dwell in a temporary residence.
13. At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree. 10.13. 14.
Studying knowledge with the mind. 10.14. 15. Constantly dwelling in the forest. 10.15.
16. One should not wander about looking at domestic animals.
17. For one who dwells constantly in the forest, whose senses are conquered, and who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses, [there is no fear].
"For one whose mind is intent on internal reflection and who is equanimous, non-returning is indeed certain. 10.17. 18.
"One whose outward signs are unmanifest, yet whose conduct is manifest. 10.18.
19. One who is not insane may wear the garb of an insane person. 10.19. 20. Furthermore, they cite this:
"Liberation is not for one who is devoted to the science of grammar."
Nor for one who delights in worldly pursuits, nor for one intent on food and clothing, nor even for one fond of pleasant dwellings. 10.20.
Neither by means of portents and omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks,
nor by instructions and discourses.
One should seek almsfood only at certain times.
(10.21) 22. One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice upon obtaining it.
One should possess only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to the objects of the senses. 10.22.
He has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to a cloth, nor to the three hollows;
he has no attachment to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food.
"Indeed, for one who knows liberation, that [is the rule]. (10.23) 24. In a Brahmin family, he should eat as much as he may obtain, both morning and evening, excluding honey and meat. (10.24) 25.
He should satisfy himself with whatever is obtained from ascetics, virtuous men, or householders. (10.25)

26. Or he may live in a village. 10.26. 27. Straightforward, free from guile, without a refuge [in worldly things], and not fickle. 10.27. 28. And he should not engage in any contact with the sense-faculties. 10.28.

29. He is indifferent toward all beings by avoiding both injury and favor. 10.29. 30. The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, censuring others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and malice is held to be the duty for all stages of life. 10.30. 31.

A Brāhmaṇa who wears the sacred thread, who carries a water-pot in his hand, who is pure, and who avoids the food of a Śūdra, does not fall from the world of Brahman—yes, from the world of Brahman. 10.31.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||10||
11.1 There are six who are worthy of the guest-offering (argha). 11.2 These are: the officiating priest, the bridegroom, the king, the paternal uncle, the graduate (snātaka), and the maternal uncle.
3. One should offer oblations into the domestic fire every morning and evening from the prepared *vaiśvadeva* food.
11.3. 4. One should present the *bali* offering to the household deities.
11.4. 5. Having given the first portion to a *śrotriya* or to a *brahmacārin*, one should thereafter give [the remainder] to the ancestors. 11.5.

6. Then one should feed the guest who is more distinguished, following the proper sequence. 11.6. 7. Among those of one's own household, [one should feed] the girls, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth. 11.7.
8. Then [he should give] other portions to those entitled to receive them.
11.8. 9. He should scatter food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, outcasts, and crows.
11.9. 10. He should give the remains of the meal, or that which is not the remains, to a *śūdra*. 11.10.
11. The remaining portion the husband and wife should eat.

11.11. 12. If a guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been prepared for all purposes, one should have special food prepared for him. 11.12. 13. For it is known [from tradition]:
The Vaiśvānara enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest;
therefore, they bring water and food for him from the rains.
"For people know that [this] is peace. (11.13) Having fed him, one should attend upon him. (11.14) One should follow him as far as the boundary, or until he gives permission to depart. (11.15)
16. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, after the fourth [lunar day], one should offer [the oblation] to the ancestors.

11.16. 17. On the preceding day, having assembled Brahmins—ascetics, householders, or virtuous men who are not of advanced age, who do not follow improper occupations, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and who are neither pupils nor resident disciples;
11.17. 18. One may also feed pupils provided they possess good qualities. 11.18.

Twice-born men [are eligible], with the exception of those who are naked, those with white teeth, those with moist teeth, those with black teeth, those afflicted by leprosy, and those with deformed nails.
11.19. Moreover, they also cite this:
"But if one is learned in the mantras and disciplined..."
Yama declared that he who is not defiled by bodily acts that corrupt the assembly is indeed a purifier of the assembly. 11.20.
At a śrāddha feast, the remnants of the food should not be removed until the end of the day.
For streams of nectar flow down;
they drink it without having performed their water-libations. (11.21) [They consume] the remnants fallen upon the ground.
One should scatter the scattering-offering and the water for anointing, and offer food to the deceased who are childless and short-lived. 11.24.
Therefore, one should offer food that has been brought, or having touched the meal, with hands that are not empty.
One should remain standing while both [sets of ancestors] have not yet finished eating.
At a rite for the gods, one should invite two; at a rite for the ancestors, three; or one from each group at both rites.
Even if one is very wealthy, one should feed [the monks] but should not be attached to a large assembly; [one should consider] the hospitality, the place, and the time. (11.27)
Purity is the perfection of a Brahmin;
these five [qualities] destroy it in detail, therefore one should avoid them. 11.28.
Or alternatively, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas and is endowed with learning and good character.
Free from all defining characteristics.
11.29–30. If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how can there be a portion for the gods (daiva) therein?
Having taken up food from the vessel for all that has been prepared, 11.30.
Having performed the *śrāddha* rite in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with it,
or else cast that food into the fire.

Or he may give it to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin). 11.31–32. As long as the food is warm, and as long as they eat with speech restrained, [so long does the offering reach the ancestors].
For the ancestors eat only so long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned. (11.32) One must not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering. (11.33)
As long as the ancestors have not yet arrived, the ancestors who have already arrived should afterwards say: "The sacrificial offering is excellent. 11.33.
But when one who has been appointed to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods discards meat,
[he incurs the sin of as many sins] as there are hairs on the animal's body.
For that long he goes to hell.
11.34–35. Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds.
And in this matter, they praise three things:
purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste—at the eighth part of the day. 11.35–36. At the eighth part of the day.
When the sun becomes dim, that time should be known as *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors at that time is inexhaustible. 11.36.
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having given or eaten at a *śrāddha*, his ancestors [suffer].
For that month, he is the consumer of the semen;
the embryo which is born from that [semen], having been given and having consumed what belongs to the father. (11.37–38)
He does not attain knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan; so too [is it for] the father and the grandfather. 11.38–39.
39. Father and grandfather indeed.
In the same way, the great-grandfather attends upon his newborn son, just as birds attend upon the peepal tree. 11.39.
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the śrāddha."
During the rainy season and under the Maghā constellation,
[one obtains] a son who increases the lineage and is intent upon the duties toward his ancestors. 11.40–41.
The ancestors rejoice in one who is endowed with devotion to the gods and the brahmins. 11.41.
His ancestors rejoice,
like farmers at a bountiful rain, when one staying at Gayā offers food.
"Your ancestors are not possessed of sons," [he says].
(11.42) One should offer [the śrāddha] to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, and on the Anvaṣṭakī day.
(11.43) Alternatively, there is no restriction regarding the time [of the offering], provided that the materials, the location, and the Brahmins are available. (11.44)

45. A Brāhmaṇa must necessarily establish the sacred fires. 11.45. 46. And he shall sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice. 11.46. 47. For this is a mandatory duty and is likewise described as a debt. 11.47.
For it is known:

"A Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: to the gods by means of sacrifice, to the ancestors by means of progeny, and to the seers by means of the life of a student (brahmacarya). He indeed is free from debt who has sacrificed, who has a son, and who has lived as a student. 11.48 One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception. 11.49
50. An eleventh year from conception for a Kṣatriya. 11.50. 51. A twelfth year from conception for a Vaiśya. 11.51. 52. Or the staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Palāśa wood. 11.52.

53. Or that of a Kṣatriya may be made of *naiyyagrodha* wood. 11.53. 54. Or that of a Vaiśya may be made of *audumbara* wood. 11.54. 55. That of a Brāhmaṇa should be equal in height to his hair. 11.55.
56. That which reaches the forehead is for the Kṣatriya.
11.56. 57. That which reaches the nose is for the Vaiśya. 11.57. The girdle made of muñja grass is for the Brāhmaṇa. 11.58.
The bowstring of a Kṣatriya is made of bowstring-fiber (dhanur-jyā). 11.59. That of a Vaiśya is made of hemp-thread (śaṇa-tāntavī). 11.60.
The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa is a black antelope skin; 11.61. that of a Kṣatriya is the skin of the Ruru deer; 11.62.
that of a Vaiśya is the skin of a cow or the skin of a goat. 11.63.
64. An unbleached white garment is for the Brāhmaṇa. 11.64. 65. A madder-red garment is for the Kṣatriya. 11.65. 66. A turmeric-yellow or silk garment is for the Vaiśya. 11.66.
67. Or, for all [castes], it may be woven cloth that is not dyed.
11.67. 68. A Brāhmaṇa should beg for alms with the word "bhavat" (sir) at the beginning. 11.68. 69. A Rājanya should beg for alms with the word "bhavat" in the middle. 11.69.
70. A Vaiśya [should marry] before the end of his [period].
11.70. 71. For a Brāhmaṇa, the time has not passed until the sixteenth year. 11.71. 72. For a Kṣatriya, [it has not passed] until the twenty-second year. 11.72.
73. Up until the twenty-fourth year, [the initiation] for a Vaiśya [is permitted].
11.73. 75. One should not initiate these [Vrātyas], nor teach them, nor officiate at sacrifices for them, nor should they marry among [their own] kin.
11.75. 76. One whose Sāvitrī has fallen away shall perform the Uddālaka-vrata. 11.76.

77. For two months he should subsist on barley-gruel (*yāvaka*); for one month on milk; for half a month on curdled milk (*āmikṣā*); for eight nights on clarified butter (*ghṛta*); for six nights on food obtained unasked; for three nights he should subsist on water; and for one day and night he should fast. 11.77. 78. He should go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
11.78. 79. Or he should perform the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice; or he should perform it—or else [he is purified]. 11.79.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||11||
12.1 Now, therefore, the observances of one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka). 12.1.1.
2. He should not beg from anyone except from kings or their attendants. 3. If overcome by hunger, he may beg for something, whether it be cultivated or uncultivated land.
Cattle, goats and sheep, and finally gold, grain, or food—
this is the instruction that a *snātaka* shall not perish from hunger. 12.3–4.
5. One should not live together with one who wears soiled clothes. 12.5. 6. Nor with one who is menstruating. 12.6. 7. Nor with one who is unfit. 12.7.
8. He shall not be one who goes from family to family. 12,8. 9. He shall not cross over a stretched-out calf-rope. 12,9. 10.
He shall not look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun. 12,10.

11. One should not void urine or excrement in water. 12. One should not spit. 13. Having wrapped one’s head and covered the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice, one should void urine and excrement facing north during the day; at night, facing south; and during the two twilights, sitting and facing north.
14. Furthermore, they also cite this:
for *snātakas*, there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper garment.
Two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water; [these are used] in water, in the hand, and on wood. 12.14–15.
It has been declared that [the vessel] is pure in fire; therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water. 12.15.
16. For Manu Prajāpati has declared this to be the "circumambulation with fire" (paryagnikaraṇa).
17. Having performed the obligatory duties...
"One should sip water for purification, O most excellent one," [says] 12.17.
One should eat food facing the east. 12.18.
19. He should swallow the entire morsel silently, with the thumb included. 12.19. 20. And he should not make a sound while eating.
12.20. 21. He should approach his own wife during the proper season, avoiding the forbidden days. 12.21.
22. He should not approach her from the side. 12.22.
23. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"But he who [approaches] her while she is holding his hand..."
If one should engage in sexual intercourse in the mouth,
his ancestors become consumers of his semen for that month.
Whatever delight there may be through constant practice is based upon the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is known in the *Kāṭhaka*: [12.23–24]
"May those among us who are about to give birth tomorrow lie with their husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra. 12.24. 25.
One should not climb a tree. 12.25. 26. One should not descend into a well. 12.26.
27. One should not blow on the fire with one's mouth.
12.27. 28. One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa. 12.28. 29. Nor between two fires. 12.29.
30. Nor [should one eat] after having obtained permission from two Brahmins.
12.30. 31. One should not eat together with one's wife; for it is known in the Vājasaneyaka that the offspring will be lacking in vigor. 12.31. 32.
One should not point out a rainbow by its name. 12.32.
33. One should say "the jeweled bow" (*maṇi-dhanuḥ*). 12,33.
34. One should avoid using a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, or a tooth-stick [made of that same wood]. 12,34.
35. One should not eat while resting on one's lap. 12.35. 36. One should not eat while sitting on a couch. 12.36. 37. One should carry a staff made of bamboo. 12.37.
38. And he may wear golden earrings. 12.38. 39. He shall not wear a garland outside [the garment], except one made of gold. 12.39.
40. He should avoid assemblies and crowds.
12.40. 41. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"And the lack of authority of the Vedas..."
"Furthermore, the disparagement of the seers and a lack of discipline in all matters— this is the destruction of the self. (12.41)
42. One should not go to a sacrifice uninvited; if one has gone, one should circumambulate it and return. 12.42. 43. One should not set out on a journey when the sun is directly over the trees.
12.43. 44. And one should not board a boat that is in a state of uncertainty [regarding its safety]. 12.44.
45. One should not cross a river by means of one's arms. 12.45. 46. Having risen during the latter part of the night and studied, one should not go back to sleep again.
12.46. 47. During the *prājāpatya* hour, a Brāhmaṇa should observe certain restraints; he should observe them, indeed he should observe them. 12.47.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||12||
13.1 Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (*svādhyāyopākarma*). It is performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or of Prauṣṭhapada.
13.2 Having established the sacred fire, he offers unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and parched grains (*dhānā*).

"To the gods, to the seers, and to the meters. (13.3) Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings and having consumed curds, they should then perform the *upākaraṇa* ceremony for the chapters of the Veda. (13.4)
5. For four and a half months, or five and a half months.
13.5. 6. After that, he should study during the bright fortnights. 13.6. 7. But he may study the Vedāṅgas at his pleasure. 13.7.
8. Its days of non-study: 13.8. 9.
During the thundering at twilight: 13.9. 10. During the twilights: 13.10.
11. In cities where there is a corpse or where the *divākīrti* (the outcaste) dwells.
13.11. 12. Or, at will, on ground smeared with cow-dung or ploughed. 13.12. 13. At the edge of a cremation ground. 13.13.
14. Of one who is lying down. 13,14. 15. Of one who has performed a *śrāddha* feast.
13,15. 16. And in this regard, they cite a verse of Manu:
Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, foodstuffs,
or whatever else may be offered at a śrāddha, there shall be a suspension of Vedic study.
"Brahmins are traditionally defined as those whose hands are their mouths.
(13.16) "Running while emitting a foul odor and so forth, or on barren soil. (13.17) "While climbing a tree. (13.18)
19. Nor on a boat or in an army. 13.19. 20. Nor from one who has eaten with wet hands. 13.20. 21. Nor when there is the sound of an arrow. 13.21.

22. On the fourteenth day, on the new moon day, on the eighth day, and during the Aṣṭakā festivals. 13.22. 23. And [the same applies] to one who has extended his feet or who has placed them in his lap. 13.23.
24. In the presence of the teacher. 13.24. 25. When free from sexual intercourse. 13.25.
26. With a garment used for sexual intercourse that has not been washed. 13.26. 27. At the edge of a village. 13.27. 28.
Of one who has vomited. 13.28.
29. [The rule applies] to that which has been uttered while one is urinating. 13.29. 30. And [it applies] to the *ṛc* and *yajus* verses when the word *sāman* is used. 13.30. 31.
When there is indigestion. 13.31.
32. During a thunderclap. 13.32. 33. During an earthquake.
13.33. 34. During an eclipse of the moon or sun. 13.34.

35. When there is a rain of stones, blood, and dust during the mountain collapses caused by the roars of the quarters, it is an untimely [rain]; [the impurity lasts] for three nights. 36. When there is a conjunction of meteors and lightning, [it lasts] for three nights. 37.
[If there is a conjunction] of meteors and lightning together with [other] celestial lights, [it lasts] for three nights.
38. In the case of a distant relative, [the impurity lasts] until the time [of the news arrives]. 39. When the teacher has died, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
40. In the case of the teacher’s son, a pupil, or a wife, [the impurity lasts] for one day and night.
40a. And among those related through officiating priests or by birth;
13.40b. one must perform the clasping of the feet of the teacher. 41.
One should rise and salute the officiating priest, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle, even if they are younger than oneself. 13.41.
42. And those who are to be honored by clasping the feet, as well as their wives and the teacher;
And the mother and father; 13,43.
44. One who knows [the rules] should say, "I am so-and-so, sir," when returning a greeting. 13,44. 45. And one who does not know [the rules]. 13,45. 46.

When a person is addressed for a return-greeting, the final vowel is protracted; a *saṃdhyakṣara* (diphthong) that is not *pragṛhya* undergoes the state of becoming *āy* or *āv*, as in "bho bhāv" (O, sir!). 13,46.
47. A father who has fallen [from his caste] is to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall because of her son. 13.47.
48. Furthermore, they also cite:
"Ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (upādhyāya) is a teacher (ācārya)..."
A father is equal to a hundred teachers, but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect. 13.48.
A wife, sons, and disciples who have become associated with sinful deeds should be rebuked and then abandoned.

13.49 One who abandons [a relative] otherwise becomes an outcaste. 13.50 A sacrificial priest or a teacher who fails to perform sacrifices or teach should be abandoned; by failing to abandon them, one falls.
13.51 They say that one born from an outcaste man is also an outcaste, except in the case of a woman.
52. For she belongs to another. 13.52. 53. He should approach her when she has no inheritance. 13.53. 54.
When the teacher’s teacher is present... 13.54.
"Conduct toward the teacher's son is desired to be like that toward the teacher; one should behave toward the teacher's son as toward the teacher"—so says the Śruti. 13.54.

55. Weapons, poison, and liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa. 13.55. 56. Learning, wealth, age, kinship, and occupation are grounds for respect. 13.56. 57. Each preceding one is more venerable than the following. 13.57.
58. When one encounters on the road an elder, a child, a sick person, a burden-carrier, a woman, or a person in a vehicle, the path must be yielded to each of them in turn.
13.58. 59. When a king and a *snātaka* meet, the path must be yielded by the king to the *snātaka*.

60. All [these things] must be provided for the bride while she is being carried away. 13.60. 61. Grass, ground, fire, water, pleasant speech, and freedom from envy—these are never lacking in the house of the virtuous, never at any time.
13.61. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. 13.
14.1 Now, therefore, we shall describe what food is fit to be eaten and what is not.
14.2 The food of physicians, hunters, unchaste women, staff-bearers (punishers), thieves, those accused of crimes, eunuchs, and outcasts is unfit to be eaten.
3. [The food] of a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, a prisoner, one afflicted by disease, a seller of *soma*, a carpenter, a washerman, a vintner, a spy, a usurer, and a leather-cutter; 14,3. 6.
He who has a paramour, and he who considers his own husband to be a paramour; 14,6. 7. And he who would burn down houses; 14,7.
8. And he who does not strike those deserving of death.
14.8. 9. Or that which is proclaimed by word of mouth: "Who shall eat? 14.9. 10. Food belonging to a group and food belonging to a courtesan. 14.10.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The gods do not eat the food of one who has a dog, nor do they eat the food of the husband of a low-caste woman."
They do not eat the food of one who is conquered by his wife, nor of one whose house is frequented by a paramour. 14.11.
12. He may accept these: fuel, water, fodder, *kuśa* grass, parched grain, a vehicle offered for his use, lodging, a *śapharī* fish, *priyaṅgu*, garlands, perfumes, honey, and meat.
14,12. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"Desiring to support his wife for the sake of his teacher..."
Desiring to honor the deities and guests,
he should accept gifts from all quarters,
but he himself should not be satisfied by that alone. 14.13.
14. The food of a hunter who goes out with arrows is not to be avoided.

14.14. For it is known that Agastya engaged in hunting during a sacrificial session lasting a thousand years; his sacrificial offerings were indeed made of the juices of excellent wild animals and birds. 14.15.
For in this regard, they also cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"Alms that are offered up, brought forward, and given without having been previously solicited— "
Prajāpati considered even those who commit evil deeds to be worthy of being fed; one should eat the food of a person who has faith.
14.16–17. One should eat the food of a person who has faith.
This applies even to a thief, and especially so to one who initiates many pupils, but never to one who performs many sacrifices for others. 14.17.
For fifteen years, his ancestors do not eat [the offerings],
nor does the fire carry his oblations.
He who treats with contempt that [woman]: 14.18.
19. [The sin] of a physician, a hunter, and a wicked surgeon who extracts arrows.
"Even if it is offered, [a gift] from a eunuch or an unchaste woman is not accepted. (14.19) "The leavings of anyone other than one's teacher are not to be eaten. (14.20)
21. One's own leavings, and that which has been defiled by the leavings of others.
And that which has been defiled by clothing, hair, or insects. 14.22.
23. However, having removed hair and insects at will, and having sprinkled [the food] with water or scattered ashes over it, one may consume it if it has been commended by word.
<41> 24. For in this regard, they also cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
The gods ordained three purifiers for the Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and [that which is purified by] fire.
And that which is praised by speech in the divine sacrificial halls, at weddings, and when sacrifices are being performed— 14.24.25.
Food touched by crows or dogs should not be discarded; therefore, one should remove that food. 14.25–26. Having removed the food, [one should sprinkle it with water].
The remainder deserves refinement: by immersion for liquid substances, but by sprinkling for solid ones. 14.26.
27. Indeed, food touched by the mouth of a cat remains pure.
28. Food that has stood overnight, food defiled by intention, food that causes heartburn, food cooked again, raw meat, and cooked meat [are forbidden].
29. However, one may consume [the meat] if it has been sprinkled with curd or clarified butter. 14.29.
30. For in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati: "Whether it be clarified butter or even oil..."
A Brahmin must not eat what has fallen off [the food] due to a fingernail;
Yama declared that to be as impure as the eating of beef. 14.30.
But those fats, salts, and condiments which have been placed directly into the hand do not reach the giver.
The eater shall indeed consume the sin.
(14.31) One should never give [food] with the hand nor with an iron vessel. (14.32)

33. For eating garlic, onions, leeks, *gṛñjana*, mushrooms, the resin of trees, blood, things cut with a weapon, food licked by dogs or crows, or the remnants of a Śūdra, one must perform the *atikṛcchra* penance.

14.33. 34. [The same applies to] the milk of a cow in heat (*sandhinī*) and the milk of a cow whose calf has not yet been born. 14.34. 35. [Also forbidden is the milk] of cows, buffaloes, and goats within ten days of calving. 14.35.
Water from a navigable river [is forbidden]. 14.36.
37. One should avoid cakes, parched grains, flour-mash, barley-meal, fried cakes, oil, milk-rice, vegetables, and fermented liquids. 14.37.
38. And other preparations made from milk and barley flour.
14.38. 39. Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the hare, the tortoise, and the monitor lizard are edible.
14.39. 40. Among domestic animals, those that do not have teeth on one side [of the mouth] are edible, with the exception of the camel. 14.40.
41. Or [the forms of] fish, cetasa, gavayas, porpoises, crocodiles, and crabs;
42. And those with deformed shapes and those with heads;
43. And the gauras, gavayas, and śarabhas.
44. Likewise, those not specifically designated [as forbidden]. 14.44. 45.
A milch-cow and a bull that have not yet cut their teeth. 14.45. 46.
However, a milch-cow and a bull are fit for consumption. 14.46.
In the Vājasaneyaka, it is known that the rhinoceros and the wild boar are pure.
Regarding these two, however, there is a dispute concerning the village pig.

And among birds, there are those born from eggs, web-footed birds, sparrows, water-fowl, swans, ruddy geese, vultures, crows, pigeons, ospreys, saranga birds, white doves, curlews, cranes, kanka birds, herons, eagles, hawks, cranes, madgu fish-eaters, lapwings, amandhalas, night-prowlers, woodpeckers, sparrows, railatas, haritas, wagtails, domestic cocks, parrots, mainas, cuckoos, and carnivorous birds.

The *viṣkira* birds—such as the *jālapāda*, *kalaviṅka*, *plava*, *haṃsa*, *cakravāka*, *bhāsa*, *vāyasa*, *pārāvata*, *kurara*, *sāraṅga*, *pāṇḍu-kapota*, *krauñca*, *krakara*, *kaṅka*, *gṛdhra*, *śyena*, *baka*, *balāka*, *madgu*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, *māndhāla*, *naktañcara*, *dārvāghāṭa*, *caṭaka*, *railātaka*, *hārīta*, *khañjarīṭa*, *grāmya-kukkuṭa*, *śuka*, *śārika*, *kokila*, and carnivorous birds—as well as those that roam in villages (*grāmacārin*) and those that frequent villages (*grāmacārin*).
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||14||
A person comes into being through the combination of blood and semen.
[The child] is for the sake of the mother and father. 15.1. 2.
In the giving away, selling, or abandoning of that [child], the mother and father have authority. 15.2. 3.
But one should not give away or receive in adoption an only son. 15.3.
4. For he [is] for the sake of the continuity of the ancestors. 15.4. 5. A woman shall neither give nor receive a son [in adoption].
Except with the permission of the husband. 15.5.

One who intends to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen and inform the king; having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* formulas in the middle of the house, he should adopt one who is a close relative rather than a distant one. 15.6.
And when a doubt arises, he should treat one who is a distant relative as if he were a *śūdra*. 15.7.
8. For it is known from scripture that by means of one person, many may be saved.

15.8. 9. If, after he has been adopted, a legitimate son (*aurasa*) should be born, the adopted son shall be entitled to a fourth part of the inheritance. 15.9. 10. Provided that he was not engaged in rites for prosperity (*abhyudayika*). 15.10.
11. An expounder of the Vedas who officiates for Śūdras and those who have fallen from the ranks of the highest varṇas—among these, the pouring out of the vessel [is prescribed]. 15.11.
12. Because of the mixing of unworthy recipients, one should take up the vessel only partially.

A slave, or the son of a woman of a different caste, or a relative who is like him but devoid of good qualities, having spread out darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward—or red grass—with his left foot, should pour out a full vessel for him. (15.12) And his kinsmen, with disheveled hair, should touch the one who pours it out. (15.13)
14. Having performed the *apasavya* rite, they may enter their homes at will. 15. From that time forward, they shall not subject him to legal proceedings.
16. Those who possess those qualities and practice that dharma [are the ones]. 15,16. 17. But for those who have fallen yet have performed the vow, there is a restoration.
15,17. 18. Now they also quote:
He should proceed as if lifting them up in front, as if playing and laughing; he should proceed as if letting them fall behind.
As if grieving, as if weeping.

(15.18) 19. Those who have killed their teacher, mother, or father may attain purification through their grace or by means of expiation; this is their restoration. (15.19) 20. Or [they are purified] by bathing in a sacred pool that flows forth from a source of merit.
Having filled either a golden vessel or one made of clay with water, they consecrate him with these waters using the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses. 15.20.
21. Every expiation for one who has been consecrated is explained by the birth of a son; it is explained, it is explained.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||15||
16.1 Now, the legal procedures.
16.2 The king or the minister shall conduct the affairs of the court.

3. When two parties are disputing, one should not take the side of either. 4. An offense is considered according to the seat [of authority] from which it is brought forward; thus is the offense determined. 5. One should be equal toward all living beings.
16.5. According to the seat [of the offender], the crime, the age, and the caste, up to the end of his education;
16.6. and he should protect what has been acquired; 16.7. as well as the property of the king and of children.
8. For those who have not attained legal capacity;
<45> 9. But when the time has arrived, he should give that [which is due] accordingly; 16,9.

Furthermore, they also cite this:
[property] inherited from a father, purchased, received as a gift, acquired by re-investment, or obtained through inheritance.
The *yajñādupagama*, the *veṇi*, and likewise the *dhūmaśikhāṣṭamī*. 16.16.
Therein, the period of ten years is [divided into] that which has been enjoyed and that which has not been enjoyed. 16.17.
Furthermore, they cite another verse:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, a sealed deposit, and women— "
The property of a king and the property of a *śrotriya* are not lost through mere possession.
(16.18) Property that has been abandoned becomes the king’s. (16.19)
20. Therefore, the king should perform his duties differently than that, together with his ministers and the citizens.

"A guaranty, a gift made in vain, what is won at dice, and what is due for spirituous liquor— "
A son is not liable to pay what remains after fines and taxes have been settled. 16.31. 32. Speak, witness, according to the truth.
Your ancestors hang suspended, rising up and falling down as they await your word. 16.32.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl,
hungry and thirsty, and blind, he should go to the house of his enemy seeking alms.

One kills a hundred horses by lying regarding a horse; one kills a thousand men by lying regarding a man; [one kills ten thousand by lying] in legal proceedings or concerning a deceased wife. 16.34–35.

At the time of marriage, during sexual union, when life is at stake, or when all one's wealth is being seized,

"Let no one sow another's seed in your field;
in the next world, the son belongs to the progenitor. The owner of the seed produces this offspring in vain. (17.9)
<48> 10. If among many men born of the same parents, only one man has a son, [then that son belongs to all].

12. Thus, there are exactly twelve types of sons as seen in the ancient tradition. 17.12. 13. The first is the son begotten by oneself upon one’s own consecrated wife. 17.13. 14. 15. The third [type of] appointed daughter (*putrikā*). 17.15. It is known that one who has no brother goes to [the lineage of] her father’s ancestors; she goes back and attains the status of a son. 17.16.
Regarding this, there is a verse:

"Whatever son is born of her shall be my son"— this is the fourth [type of son], the *paunarbhava*. 17.18.

19. She who, having abandoned her husband from her youth and having lived with others, returns to his very household, is a *punarbhū*. 17.19. 20. And she who, having abandoned a husband who is impotent, fallen [from caste], or insane, finds another husband, or does so after he has died, is a *punarbhū*. 17.20. 21. The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) is the fifth. 17.21.
22. They say that if a mother, while still in her father’s house and not yet consecrated [in marriage], should procreate a son out of desire, he becomes the son of her maternal grandfather.
23. Furthermore, they cite this:
"The daughter who has not been given away in marriage by him..."
"One should obtain a son from one of equal status;
through him, a daughter's son shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his wealth. (17.23)
24. And the one secretly born in the house is the sixth. 17.24.
25. Thus.
"These are the heirs, the kinsmen,
the saviors from great fear," so they say. 17,25.
26. Now, among those who have no heirs or kinsmen, the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*) is the first [in right of succession]. 17.26. 27. A woman who is married while already pregnant...
The son born together [with the wife] is the first; 17.27. The second is the adopted son (dattaka); 17.28.
He whom the mother and father may give away; 17.29.
30. The third [case] is that of the purchased one.
17.30. 31. This has been explained by means of the story of Śunaḥśepa.
17.31. 32. King Hariścandra indeed purchased the son of Ajīgarta Sauyavasi. 17.32.

33. The fourth [type of son] is he who comes of his own accord. 17.33. 34. This has been explained by means of the story of Śunaḥśepa. 17.34. 35. The officiating priests said, "Let this boy be mine alone as a son," but he did not agree to them. They then reached an agreement, saying, "Let him be the son of whomever he desires. Viśvāmitra was his *hotṛ* priest, and thus he attained the status of his son. 17.35.

36. The fifth is the *apaviddha* (cast-off). 17.36. 37. He whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by his mother and father. 17.37. 38. They say that the son of a *śūdra* woman is indeed the sixth. 17.38.
Thus, these are the non-heirs and non-relatives.
(17.38) Furthermore, they also cite this:
"If none of the six ancestors of anyone should have an heir, these [others] shall take his inheritance. (17.39)
40. Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers.
41. And those [wives] who are childless [shall have their shares] until the birth of a son.
42. The eldest shall take two shares. 17.42. 43. And of the cattle and horses, he shall take every tenth. 17.43. 44. Goats, sheep, and the house belong to the youngest. 17.44.
45. Iron implements and tools belong to the middle son.
17.45. 46. The mother’s dowry the women shall divide among themselves.
17.46. 47. If a Brāhmaṇa has sons by wives of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes... 17.47.
48. The son of a Brāhmaṇī woman shall take three shares.
49. The son of a Rājanyā woman shall take two shares. 50. The others shall divide the remainder equally.
51. And he by whom this [property] was personally acquired shall take two shares for himself.
52. But those who have entered another stage of life (āśrama) are entitled to no share. 53. Nor are eunuchs, the insane, and outcasts entitled to a share.
54. The maintenance of the impotent and the insane [is the duty of their relatives].
17.54. 55. The widow of a deceased man shall observe a vow for six months, eating food free from salt and pungent seasonings, and sleeping on the ground. 17.55.

56. After six months have passed, having bathed and offered the *śrāddha* for her husband, and having assembled those related by learning, ritual action, teacher, or kinship, the father or brother shall arrange the *niyoga*. 17.56. 57. One should not appoint a woman who is insane, lacking self-control, or diseased. 17.57. 58. Nor one who is older [than the man]. 17.58.
59. Sixteen years. 17,59. 60. Unless he should be afflicted by disease. 17,60.
61. During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, she should behave like a bride, except for laughing, harshness of speech, and harshness of physical punishment.
17.61. 62. She should go first to [partake of] food, clothing, bathing, and ointments. 17.62. 63.
They say that if a son is born from a woman who has not been authorized, he belongs to the progenitor. 17.63.
64. If there should be two [widows] eligible for appointment (niyoga), [the elder shall be appointed].
17.64. 65. There is no appointment [of a widow] out of greed for inheritance.
17.65. 66. Or, some say that one may appoint her after having prescribed an expiation (prāyaścitta). 17.66.
67. A maiden who has reached puberty shall wait for three years.
68. After three years, she may find a husband of equal status.
69. Furthermore, they also cite this:
But if, due to the father’s negligence, a girl here is given away after she has passed the proper measure of her age,
she, while awaiting [her husband], destroys the giver.
Excessive delay is like a teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā) [left unpaid].
17.69–70. Out of fear that the period of fertility (*ṛtu-kāla*) might pass, a father should give away his daughter while she is still a girl (*nagnikā*).
For while she remains in her season, the fault falls upon the father; as many seasons as touch the maiden [so many does he incur]. 17.70–71.
When a woman who desires [a man] is solicited by those of equal status,
it is a declaration of Dharma that as many embryos as have been conceived by those two— mother and father— have been destroyed by them. 17.71.
If, after she has been given with water and words, the groom should die first,
she is not considered wedded by the performance of the mantras.
A maiden belongs to her father alone; if she is forcibly carried off, [he may reclaim her]. 17.72.
If a maiden has been taken by force...
If she has not been consecrated by mantras, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule;
she is just like a maiden. 17.73.
If the husband has died while she was still a young girl,
having been consecrated by mantras alone,
provided that her virginity remains intact;
She is eligible for remarriage. 17.74.
A wife whose husband has gone abroad shall wait for five years. 17.75. After five years have passed, she may go to her husband’s presence. 17.76.

77. If she is not desirous of departing for the sake of dharma or wealth, she should behave as if she were already dead. 17.77. 79. From this point forward, among those who share the same purpose, birth, funeral rice-ball offerings, water libations, and lineage, each preceding one is more venerable than the next. 17.79. 80. However, while a man of noble family is available, she must not go to another. 17.80.

81. If none of the six preceding [relatives] should be an heir to someone, his sapindas or those standing in the place of sons shall divide his property. 17.81. 82. In their absence, the teacher and the pupil shall take it. 17.82. 83. In their absence, the king shall take it. 17.83.

84. But a king must not take the property of a Brāhmaṇa. 17.84. 85. For the property of a Brāhmaṇa is terrible poison. 17.85. 86. They say that poison is not truly poison; [the property of a Brāhmaṇa is the real poison]. 17.86.
"The property of a Brahmin is called poison;

<53> 87. He should bestow [it] upon those virtuous men who have mastered the three Vedas; he should bestow it.

18.1 It is said that one born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Caṇḍāla. 18.2 One born of a Rājanyā woman [from a Śūdra father] becomes a Vaiṇa.

gold, a cow, or a garment is the sacrificial fee. 18.16.

5. Because of protecting both.
19,5. 6. And because of incapacity [otherwise].

19.8. 9. Punishment, however, should be determined according to the specific circumstances of place, time, social duty (*dharma*), age, learning, and station, as well as the nature of the injury or verbal abuse.
19.9. 10. This is established through both traditional authority (*āgama*) and illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). 19.10.

11. One should not harm trees that bear flowers and fruit. 19,11. However, one may cut them down for the purpose of cultivation. 19,12. And [one may harm them] for the sake of the components of domestic life.

19. One should cause men to pay at least one hundred [paṇas] as a fine.

22. A tree that has no water [nearby] is exempt from tax.

19.22. 23. One who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a king’s servant, one without a protector, a renunciant, a child, an elderly person, a youth, and a woman who has recently given birth; 19.23. 24.
Maidens traveling toward their future husbands and women whose husbands have been hired out for labor; 19.24.

28. He shall cause the monthly marriage-fee to be brought to him. 19.28. 29. And when the king has died, he shall pay the incidental fee. 19.29. 30. By this, the maintenance of the mother is explained. 19.30.
The king shall support the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle of the queen; (32) as well as their kinsmen and others. 19.31–32.

36. Because the inheritance goes to him. 19.36. 37. Regarding the marriage-fee (*śulka*), they also cite this verse of Manu:

Not for one engaged in a craft, nor for a child, nor for a messenger;
not for what is obtained by begging, nor for the remnants of an oblation, nor for a learned Vedic scholar, nor for a renunciant, nor at a sacrifice. 19.37.

38. A thief is not considered guilty [of the full offense] if he entered [the house] by stealth. 39. One who carries a weapon and is caught with the stolen goods is [guilty]; however, according to some, this applies only if he is wounded. 40. Upon releasing one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night.
41. The domestic priest shall fast for three nights. 19.41. 42.

Moreover, they also cite this:
"The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband."
The disciple and the sacrificer transfer their guilt to the teacher;
the thief transfers his guilt to the king. But those who have been punished by kings [are purified]. 19.44–45.
Having committed evil deeds, men go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. 19.45.
The king incurs this sin when he releases one who is guilty.

[This applies] to kings in matters of urgent necessity.

48. And in this regard, they cite a verse sung by Yama:

For those who worship the station of Indra become, indeed, one with Brahman forever—
forever, indeed. 19.48.
