20.1 One who has been caught looking at the rising sun, one who has been caught looking at the setting sun, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who has superseded his younger brother in marriage, one who is superseded by his older brother, one whose younger sister is married before him, one who marries while his elder sister remains unmarried, a slayer of a hero, and one who abandons the Veda— these are the sinners. (1.18) [The same sequence, but without penalties:]
There is expiation for an offense committed unintentionally;
some say there is also [expiation] for one committed intentionally.
The teacher is the instructor of those who possess self-control.
The teacher of the evil-minded is the king; but the teacher of those whose sins are concealed is Yama, the son of Vivasvat. 20,3.
And there, having risen with the sun, he should remain standing during the day and mutter the Sāvitrī. 20.4.
Thus, he remained deprived of the sun during the night. (20.5) As for the one with deformed nails and dark teeth:

He shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights. (20.6) The elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (the *parivitti*) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then enter the household state, and marry that very same woman. (20.7) Now, the younger brother who marries before his elder (the *parivividāna*) shall perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances, give her back to the elder, and then enter the household state again and marry that very same woman. (20.8)

A man who marries a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then marry a wife, and subsequently take that [younger sister] as his wife. 20.9.
10. A man who has married a woman whose husband was previously married shall perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances, give her back to her [former] husband, and then marry again. 20.10.
11. We shall explain the penance for killing a hero later. 20.11. 12.
One who has forsaken the Veda, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, may receive the Veda again from his teacher. 20.12. 13.

One who has violated the bed of his Guru, having extracted his penis together with the testicles and placed it in his joined palms, should walk facing south; wherever he meets with an obstacle, there he should remain until his body perishes. 20.13.
14. Or, having been stripped of his clothes and smeared with clarified butter, he should embrace a red-hot iron image; it is known from tradition that he becomes purified through death.
15. The same applies to the wives of one's teacher, son, or pupil. 16. [The same applies] to women of the womb.
Having approached a heavy female friend, a friend of a guru, one who is an unfit recipient, or one who has fallen, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one quarter of a year. 20.16.

17. And this same [penance] applies to eating the food of a *caṇḍāla* or one who has fallen from his caste; however, there is a re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*), with the exclusion of shaving and the other [rites].
20.17. 18. And in this regard, they cite a verse of Manu:
"Shaving, the girdle, the staff..."
The practice of begging for alms and the religious vows— these, however, are subject to re-consecration through the rite of re-ordination. 20.18.

19. If one knowingly trades in *asurā* liquor or unknowingly consumes *surā* liquor, one must perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and undergo the purificatory rite (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*) again.
20.19. And the same applies to the consumption of urine, feces, or semen. 20.20.
If any twice-born man should drink water that has been kept in a vessel for liquor,
he should drink water from the leaves of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, and the palāśa.
He becomes pure in just three nights.
(20.21) But in the case of repeated practice regarding *surā*, a twice-born man shall drink that [liquor] when it is fire-colored; he becomes purified through death.

(20.22) We shall now declare [the penance for] killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); by killing a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a killer of an embryo, as does one who kills an embryo that is not yet known [as male or female]. (20.23)

24. For embryos are not yet known as males; therefore, they offer oblations for the sake of producing a male. 20.24. 25. A killer of an embryo, having kindled the fire, should offer these [oblations]. 20.25. 26. "I offer the body hairs to Death. 20.26.
"By means of the body hairs, I cause Death to dwell"— with these words he offers the first [oblation];
"I sacrifice the skin of Death."
"O skin, clothe death"— with this he offers the second oblation; "I offer the blood to Death."
"May death dwell in blood"— with these words he offers the third oblation;
"I offer the flesh of death."
"May I dwell with death through flesh"— this is the fourth [offering];
"I offer the sinews to death."
"By means of the sinews, I clothe Death"— with these words he offers the fifth oblation;
"I offer fat to Death."
"By means of fat, I cause death to dwell," with this he offers the sixth oblation; "I offer the bones to death."
"By means of the bones, I cause Death to dwell"— with these words he offers the seventh [oblation]; "I offer the marrow to Death."
"By means of the marrow, cause Death to dwell [within you]"—this is the eighth [verse].
(20.26) One should cause oneself to be slain facing the enemy in battle for the sake of a king or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa. (20.27)
28. For it is known from tradition that one who has committed an offense becomes purified after three times [repeating the rite], even if he was not previously conquered [by the sin]. 20.28. 29.
For it is said that the transgression becomes diminished. 20.29.
Nevertheless, they cite this example:
"Having said 'He is fallen,' [one becomes] fallen."
Whether one calls a thief a "thief" or otherwise, by such speech one incurs an equal fault;
falsely so, one would incur a twofold fault. (20.30)
31. Having killed a Kṣatriya in this manner, one shall perform [the penance] for eight years. 20.31. 32. Six years for a Vaiśya. 20.32. 33. Three years for a Śūdra. 20.33.
34. Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an Ātreyī, as well as a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a Soma sacrifice.
20.34. 35. We shall explain the Ātreyī: they say an Ātreyī is a woman who has her menses and has bathed after her period.
20.35. 36. For it is said that the husband and wife are to come together during this [period]. 20.36.

37. [The penance prescribed for killing] a non-Ātreyī woman applies in the case of injuring a Kṣatriya. 20.37. 38. [The penance prescribed for killing] a Kṣatriya woman applies in the case of injuring a Vaiśya. 20.38. 39. [The penance prescribed for killing] a Vaiśya woman applies in the case of injuring a Śūdra. 20.39.

40. Having killed a Śūdra woman, [one must perform penance] for one year. 20.40. 41. For the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, having disheveled his hair, he should run toward the king, saying: "I am a thief, O Lord; may you punish me. The king should give him an axe of Udumbara wood; with that he should take his own life. It is known from tradition that by death he becomes purified. 20.41. 42.
Or, being naked and smeared with ghee, he should burn himself with a fire of cow-dung, starting from the feet. It is known from tradition that by death he becomes purified. 20.42.
Furthermore, they cite this:
regarding those who died long ago due to evil and various types of actions, [the following is said].
Furthermore, listen to how it becomes a limb for those who have entered a body again: a thief becomes one with deformed nails. 20.43–44.
44. A thief becomes one with deformed nails.
The killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with white leprosy; the drinker of spirituous liquor has black teeth; and the violator of the Guru's bed suffers from skin disease. (20.44)
Furthermore, in the case of association with outcasts—whether through Vedic study or marriage—one must renounce those portions of knowledge obtained from them and shall not dwell together with them.
46. It is known from tradition that by going toward the northern direction and studying the *Saṃhitā* while fasting, one becomes purified.
Nevertheless, they cite this:
"By the mortification of the body, by austerity, and by study..."
"It is known, it is known: 'The evildoer is released from evil, and by giving, he is also released. 20.47.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||20||

21.1 If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in vīraṇa grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī’s head, she should be anointed with oil, stripped naked, mounted upon a black donkey, and paraded along the high road. Thus it is known: "She becomes purified."

If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red darbha grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇa woman's head, she should be anointed with oil, led naked upon a white donkey along the high road, and it is declared that she thereby becomes purified. 21.2.

3. If a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap that Kṣatriya in reed-leaves and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī’s head, she should be anointed with oil, placed naked upon a white donkey, and made to walk along the high road. It is traditionally known that she thus becomes purified. 21.3. 4. In the same manner, [the penance applies] when a Vaiśya [has intercourse] with a Kṣatriya woman.

5. And a Śūdra [is the same] for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman. 6. In the case of transgression against her husband by means of thought alone, she should eat barley-gruel or milk-and-rice for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, having immersed herself in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse for each head (of the fire). It is traditionally known that she becomes purified. 7.

In the case of verbal intimacy, having performed this very same penance for a month, after the month she should, having immersed herself in water, offer oblations with four times one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse for each head. It is traditionally known that she becomes purified.

8. In the case of sexual intercourse, however, one should wear a garment smeared with ghee for one year, or sleep on a bed of kusha grass within a pit filled with cow dung; after a year has passed, one should offer oblations of one's head with the Sāvitrī mantra recited one hundred and eight times while submerged in water; thus it is known that she becomes purified. 21.8. 9.
In the case of sexual intercourse, she is excluded from going to sacred fords (tīrthas) and from religious duties (dharmas). 21.9.
But four [wives] must be abandoned: one who has gone to a disciple, one who has gone to a teacher, one who kills her husband, and especially one who is unchaste.
And she who has approached one who is censured: even if she be a Brāhmaṇī woman here who has drunk liquor,
the gods do not lead her to the world of her husband.
Right here she moves about, her merit exhausted; she becomes like a pearl-oyster shell in the water. (21.11) [Of] the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas. (21.12)
Women who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. 21.12.
13. They should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa in reverse order. 14. [This applies to] those women devoted to their husbands who maintain the household.
For those who observe the vow of truth and the vow of purity, their worlds are equal to those of their husbands; but for the unchaste women, there are the worlds of jackals. 21.14.
Half the body of that man falls [to hell] whose wife drinks liquor.
No atonement is prescribed for one whose body is half-fallen [from caste]. 21.15.

If a Brāhmaṇa should unintentionally approach the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance if his religious duties have not ceased, and the Atikṛcchra penance if his religious duties have ceased. 21.16.
17. The same applies to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.

21.17. 18. If he should kill a cow, he must remain wrapped in her raw hide for six months, performing either the Kṛcchra or the Tapta-kṛcchra penance. 21.18. 19. This is the rule for those two [castes]. 21.19.
For three days he eats during the day, for another three days he eats only at night,
and for three days he observes the vow of eating only what is unasked for.
Not eating for three days constitutes the *kṛcchra* penance.
For three days one should drink hot water;
for three days one should drink hot milk.
Having drunk hot ghee for three days and subsisting on air for the following three days— this is the *taptakṛcchra*. 21.21.
22. And one should give [an oblation] in a bull-shaped vessel. 21, 22.
23. Moreover, they also cite: "In ancient times, there were only three diseases."
Envy, fasting, old age,
and the killing of a spotted goat— one should bring back ninety-eight [of these]. 21.23.

24. Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, or a mouse, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift. 21.24. 25. But having killed a heap of boneless creatures as large as a cow, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift. 21.25. 26. But for each individual creature possessing bones, [the penance is] the same. 21.26.
27. He who should cast away the sacred fires shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then have the fires re-established.

21.27. 28. In the event of persistent falsehood toward a teacher, one should bathe with one's clothes on and propitiate the teacher; it is known from tradition that through his favor one becomes purified. 21.28.

29. An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism. 21.29. 30. But one who lives by the conduct of an atheist shall perform the *atikṛcchra*. 21.30. 31. By this, the seller of *soma* is explained. 21.31.
32. A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), upon breaking his vow of initiation (*dīkṣā*), shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and then increase his hair and beard in a great thicket.

21.32. 33. For mendicants (*bhikṣukas*), like forest-dwellers, there is the increasing of the Soma and the performance of purificatory rites according to their own scriptures; and the performance of purificatory rites according to their own scriptures.
21.33. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. 21.

22.1 Now, this man indeed gives false testimony, or he officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed, or he accepts what should not be accepted, or he eats what is unfit to be eaten, or he practices what is improper to practice. 22.2 Regarding this, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not.
3. "One should not perform [it]," so they say. 22,3. 4. "For action does not perish," [they say]. 22,4. 5.
Therefore, one should indeed perform it, according to the evidence of the Śruti. 22,5.
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin" (22.6).
And likewise, "one who is accused [of a crime] should perform the Gosava or the Agniṣṭut sacrifice" (22.7).
8. The means of expiation for that [sin] are recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), burnt offerings (*homa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and giving gifts (*dāna*).

9. The *Upaniṣads*, the beginnings of the Vedas, the ends of the Vedas (*vedānta*), the *Saṃhitās* of all the Vedic meters, the *Madhu* hymns, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājana* and *Rauhiṇa* *Sāmans*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānī* verses, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers (*pāvana*).
10. Now they also cite this:
Performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice once during each season.
"He purifies ten generations.

(22.10) By the rule of fasting, drinking milk, subsisting on fruit, eating *yāvaka* (barley gruel) from the hollow of the hand, consuming gold, and drinking *soma*—these are means of purification (*medhya*).
(22.11) All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords (*tīrtha*), dwellings of seers (*ṛṣi*), cow-pens, and crossroads—these are sacred places (*deśa*). (22.12)
13. The years, the months, twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, and a day and night are the [periods of] time.
22.13. 14. These very [periods] shall be performed optionally when no specific instruction is given.
22.14. 15. In the case of heavy sins, heavy [penances]; in the case of light [sins], light [penances]. 22.15.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation; this is the universal expiation.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||22||
23.1 If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he shall sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas deities in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest.
23.2 Or he may offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) dedicated to Nirṛti.

3. For that [transgression], he should offer oblations, saying: "To Desire, svāhā! To the one who desires desire, svāhā! To Nairṛtī, svāhā! To the deities who are Rākṣasas, svāhā! (23.3). 4. This same [penance applies] for the emission of semen during the day while dreaming, or at the conclusion of vows prior to the *samāvartana* ceremony. (23.4). 5.
In the case of sexual intercourse with an animal, he should give a white bull as a gift. (23.5).
6. Having gone to a cow, the offense is explained as being equal to the killing of a Śūdra.
23.6. 7. For a religious student (brahmacārin) who performs the funeral rites [for someone other than his parents], there is a cessation from his vows.
23.7. 8. Except in the case of [the funeral rites for] his mother or father. 23.8.
9. If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remnants of his teacher's food for the sake of medicine.
10. If he should die while being employed by his teacher, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
11. If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat, having performed a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance involving the eating of leavings, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
12. And likewise in the case of eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony or during a period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*).
13. It is known from the *Vājasaneyaka* that honey which has been removed [from its source] unintentionally does not cause defilement. 23.13.

24. Having touched human bone that is oily (fatty), there is impurity for three nights. 23,24. 25. But if it is not oily, there is impurity for one day and night. 23,25. 26. And likewise when following a corpse. 23,26.
For those engaged in Vedic study, there shall be a fast for one day and night upon passing between them.
28. There shall be a three-night fast, ritual bathing, and mutual separation from each other.
29. For eating [the meat] of a dog, a cat, a mongoose, or a swift-moving [animal], the penance lasts for one day and night.

23.29. 30. For eating the flesh of a dog, a cock, a domestic pig, a heron, a vulture, a bearded vulture, a pigeon, a human, a crow, or an owl, there shall be a fast for seven nights, becoming void of feces, consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and undergoing the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). 23.30. 31. But a Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog...
"Having gone to a river that flows to the ocean,
having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and having consumed clarified butter, one then becomes pure. (23.31)
Time, fire, purification by the mind, looking at water and the sun,
and ignorance of living beings [are the means of purification].
Sixfold purification is prescribed. 23.32.
It is known from tradition that upon touching a dog or a *cāṇḍāla*, one becomes pure immediately by bathing with one's clothes on. 23.33.
Upon hearing the cry of an outcaste (*patita*) or a *cāṇḍāla*, they should remain for three nights observing silence and abstaining from food. 23.34.
35. It is known from tradition that those who practice this [recitation] up to ten thousand times become purified.

23.35. 36. By this very [rule], those who teach for a fee and those who officiate as priests for a fee are explained; it is known from tradition that they also become purified by the renunciation of their fees.
23.36. 37. By this very [rule], one who is falsely accused is also explained. 23.37.
38. For the murder of an embryo, one should subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights.
39. Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime entailing loss of caste or of a lesser crime, one should subsist on water for a month and recite the Śuddhavatī verses.
40. Or he may go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
23.40. 41. By this very [rule], intercourse with a *caṇḍāla* woman is explained.
23.41. 42. Now, another general rule for the *kṛcchra* penance is set forth. 23.42.
One day in the morning, one day by night, and one day without begging;
this constitutes one *parāka* ritual cycle.
Likewise, for the next four days,
Manu, the best of those who uphold the Dharma, [prescribed this] for the sake of favoring the Brahmins.
Thus he spoke regarding the hardship for children among the young, the old, and the sick.
Now follows the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month,
one should eat fourteen morsels;
one should be a consumer who increases the number of morsels.
One should complete the remainder of the fortnight;
for in this way, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, one should consume only a single morsel.
He should eat while diminishing his morsels and complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In this very state, he should either sing the Sāman chants or mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
This is the Cāndrāyaṇa month,
a purifier praised by the sages,
[to be applied] in all cases where no specific penance has been prescribed.
An expiation is prescribed. It is prescribed. (23.47).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. [23]
24.1 Now follows the *atikṛcchra* (the most difficult penance).

24.2 Eating [only] in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening, and eating what is unasked for during the *parāka*—this is the *kṛcchra*; one should eat as much as one could take in a single mouthful, as described before; that is the *atikṛcchra*.
<70> 3. Abstaining from food is the *kṛcchra*; that [same practice] is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. 24,3. 4. These are the forms of the vows for the *kṛcchras*. 24,4.

5. He should have his beard and hair shaved, except for the eyebrows, the eyelashes, and the top-knot; having trimmed his nails, wearing a single garment, eating blameless food, begging for alms once [a day], bathing three times a day, carrying a staff and a water-pot, avoiding conversation with women and Śūdras, and habitually standing during the day and sitting at night—thus says the venerable Vasiṣṭha. 24.5.

6. He shall not give this Dharmaśāstra to one who is not his son, nor to one who is not his disciple, nor to one who has not resided with him for a year. 7. The sacrificial fee is a thousand [cows], eleven bulls, or it may be the favor of the teacher; or it may be the favor of the teacher.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
25.1 Likewise, for great sins whose faults have not been made public, [there is no purification].
I shall explain, without omission, the purification for all minor offenses,
Whether he be an elder or even a learned man,
other people [should not reveal] the expiation spoken in secret as previously described. 25.2.
3. By means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), purifications, gifts, burnt offerings (homa), and likewise recitations (japa),
those who are disciplined are liberated.
There is no doubt that one is freed from sins. 25.3.
4. Likewise, the purifying breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), the sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis), and the syllable Om (praṇava)—
Seated with the *pavitra* in his hand, he should practice the daily *brahman*. 25.4.
Constantly engaged and practicing breath control again and again, [he should do so] from the tips of his body hairs to the tips of his nails.
Let him perform supreme austerity. From suppression arises wind;
from wind, indeed, fire is born.
Then, by means of heat, the waters are driven forth;
thus, through these three, one is purified within. (25.6) Not by intense asceticism alone... (25.7)
O twice-born ones, neither by Vedic recitation nor by sacrifice are they able to go to that destination which they reach through yoga. 25.7.
Through yoga, knowledge is attained;
yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma;
yoga is eternal supreme austerity.
Therefore, one should always be disciplined.
25.8. 9. One should be constantly engaged with the *praṇava* and with the seven *vyāhṛtis*.
In the three-footed Gāyatrī,
no fear exists anywhere;
likewise, the Vedas begin with the syllable Om.
All things are established in the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* consists of all speech; therefore, one should practice the *praṇava*. 25.10.
11. The single syllable is known as the supreme Brahman, the highest purifier. 12. Of all sins indeed...
When such a confusion has arisen,
the great purification is ten thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra. 25.12.
With the breath restrained, one should recite three times the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras.
That is called *prāṇāyāma*. That is called [it]. 25.13.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. 25.
26.1 One who is not bound by worldly constraints should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the prescribed rule.
The evil committed during day and night perishes at that very moment. 26,1.
Whatever sin has been committed by deed, thought, or word during the day,
one should sit for the evening twilight prayer (sandhyā).
One removes the sin committed by deed, mind, or speech during the night through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 26.2.3.
Standing during the morning twilight,
one dispels [the sins] through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava. 26,3.4.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), performed day after day for a month, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin. 26.4.
Having recited this [hymn] of Kautsa, one should approach the three verses of Vasiṣṭha beginning with "apeta," as well as the Māhitra and the Śuddhavatī verses.
Even a drinker of *surā* is purified by reciting the *Āsyavāmīya*, the *Śivasankalpa*, and likewise [the *Puruṣasūkta*]. 26.5.6. Having muttered these, he is cleansed.
Even after stealing gold, one becomes stainless in an instant by practicing this *haviṣyanti* [verse]. 26,6. 7. Having practiced this *haviṣyanti*.
By reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with "na taṃ mahi" and the Puruṣa Sūkta, one who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated. 26.7.
Alternatively, while immersing oneself in water,
one should recite the Avamarṣaṇa hymn three times, just as at the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
Manu has declared such a thing. 26.8.
9. A sacrifice consisting of recitation is ten times superior to a sacrifice consisting of ritual action.
The whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold [more effective],
and the mental recitation is remembered as a thousandfold.
(26.9) As for those four *pākayajñas*...
All those [performers] endowed with ritual sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña). 26.10.
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
He may perform other rites, or he may not.
The benevolent one is called a brahmin; [this applies] to those who recite mantras and those who perform fire-offerings.
<73> 12. To those who recite and to those who offer oblations.
Sins do not dwell among those who meditate, those who dwell at sacred fords,
and those who have performed ablutions with head-vows. 26.12.
Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
so too does one who is constantly devoted to silent recitation.
The Brahmin blazes forth. 26.13.
14. [This is for] those who constantly study their own sacred texts and whose selves are ever disciplined.
For those who recite it and offer oblations,
no downfall exists;
[one should recite] the Goddess up to a thousand times.
One who desires purification should employ [this rite] consisting of at least ten and up to one hundred [verses], even if he stands guilty of all sins. 26.15.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own adversity through the strength of his arms, while a Vaiśya and a Śūdra should do so through wealth.
Through recitations and burnt offerings, O best of the twice-born, [one attains success]. Just as horses would be without a chariot, or a chariot without horses;
Thus, austerity for one who lacks knowledge, or knowledge for one who lacks austerity, is like food mixed with honey. 26.17–18.
Honey combined with food— likewise, austerity and knowledge joined together constitute a great medicine. 26.18.
A Brahmin who is endowed with learning and austerity, even if he performs sinful deeds, is always purified by his daily recitation of sacred texts.
"He is not joined with sin;
he is not joined with sin.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||26||
27.1 Even if more than a hundred improper deeds have been committed, if the Veda is retained [in memory], [one is purified].
All that the fire of his knowledge burns away for him, just as ordinary fire consumes fuel. 27.1.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so too does the fire of the Vedas burn.
Having destroyed the fault of his own karma born of action,
even if he were to destroy these worlds and enjoy them from here and there, [he remains untainted].
The wise man who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever;
One may delight in evil deeds;
through ignorance and negligence, one is consumed by that karma and nothing else. 27.4.
The sage who performs austerities in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits,
and who studies even a single verse of the Rigveda— [the latter is superior].
That [Veda] and those [Itihāsas and Purāṇas] are equal to it.
27.5. One should augment the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me.
The sequence of performing the great sacrifices according to one's capacity quickly destroys even those sins born of the great transgressions. 27.7.

8. One should constantly perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas, without being dependent on external motives; for by performing that according to one's ability, [one attains the highest goal].
One attains the supreme goal. 27.8.
9 From officiating at sacrifices, from teaching, from marriage alliances, and likewise from the acceptance of improper gifts, [one falls].
There would be no fault in [giving] to Brahmins,
for he is equal to fire and the sun;
this applies when [the recipient] has arisen in the place of a conch-shell.
Regarding what is considered unfit for consumption and what is fit for consumption, I shall speak of the purity of food; listen to me as I declare it. 27.10.
One should drink Brāhmī, Suvarcalā, and Śaṅkhapuṣpī— dry and free from pungent and salty flavors— for three nights.
The Brāhmaṇa [should offer] with milk. 27.11.
12. Palāśa leaves, bilva leaves, kuśa grass, lotuses, and udumbara leaves.
Having boiled water, one should drink it;
one becomes pure in exactly three nights. 27.12.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
along with a fast for one night.
One may even purify an outcaste dog-cooker (śvapāka).
27.13–14. Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter—
Having consumed that for five nights, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); likewise, one who consumes barley according to the prescribed rule [is purified]. 27.14–15.
One is purified by direct perception alone;
those who possess a pure state of being are pure, but in the absence of purity, they remain full of passion. 27.15.
16. One should likewise eat three morning meals and three evening meals consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya), and similarly, one may subsist on food that is unasked for.
There should be three fasts. 27.16. 17. Now, if he hastens to perform them, he should subsist on air for a day.
Having stayed overnight at a body of water,
that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance; likewise,
eight thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī mantra.
Having performed the recitation when the sun has risen,
one is liberated from all sins, provided one is not a slayer of a Brahmin. 27.18.
19. Indeed, whether one is a thief, a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher's bed— having studied the Dharmaśāstra itself...
One is liberated from all transgressions; likewise, from misfortunes, ill-performed rites, and great evils. 27.19–20.
The Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances indeed destroy all sins.
One should increase the food morsel by one each day.
One should decrease [the portions] during both the bright and dark fortnights; on the day of non-existence (amāvāsyā), one should not eat at all—
such is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa.
And thus is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
A woman is not defiled by a paramour.
A Brahmin is not defiled by the performance of rites for the gods;
water is not defiled by urine or excrement;
nor is fire defiled by the act of burning. 28.1.
Whether she has gone astray of her own accord, or has been abandoned by her husband, or has been enjoyed by force or through coercion.
Even if she has fallen into the hands of a thief,
a defiled woman must not be abandoned;
her abandonment is not prescribed.
One should attend upon her during the time of her menses;
she becomes pure through the ritual union at the proper season. Women are an incomparable means of purification.
These women are never defiled;
for month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds. 28.4.
In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods— Soma, Gandharva, and Vahni— and only afterwards did they go to human beings.
These women became subject to impurity according to the nature of things.
To them, Soma gave purity,
and Gandharva taught the art of speech.
And because fire is the means by which everything becomes pure, women are therefore free from blemish. (28.6) There are three sins of women.

Those in the world who know the Dharma understand that the killing of one's husband and the causing of an abortion— bringing down one's own embryo— are [equivalent to] the murder of a learned Brahmin. 28.7.
A calf is pure at the source of its mother's milk,
a bird while causing fruit to fall, and women during sexual union.
A dog is pure when seizing game. (28.8) Goats and horses are pure in their mouths; cows, however, are pure in every part. (28.9)
10. Hereafter, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas,
by the recitation and the fire-offerings of which—
They are purified; of this there is no doubt. 28.10.
11. [The hymns] Aghamarṣaṇa, Devakṛta, Śuddhavatyaḥ, and the Taratsamāḥ.
The Kūṣmāṇḍa hymns, the Pāvamānī verses, and likewise the Durgā-Sāvitrī. 28.11.
The *atiṣaṅgas*, the *padastobhas*, the *sāmans*, as well as the *vyāhṛtis* and the *bhāruṇḍa-sāmans*.
The Gāyatra, the Raivata, as well as the Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa,
and likewise the Devavratas.
The Ab-liṅga, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāk-sūkta, the Madhu-ṛcs, the Śatarudriya, and the Atharvaśiras. 28.13–14.
The Trisuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans, Śuddhāśuddhīye. 28.14.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner Vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these, when recited, purify living beings.
If one so desires, one obtains the recollection of past births.
28.15–16. Gold is the first offspring of Agni;
the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
He who would give gold, a cow, and land would obtain an infinite reward for those [gifts]. (28.16) 17.
[Those who obstruct] hinder the donor.
A cow, a horse, gold, and land—
these are [given] when one sees the hand of a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas and has been rejected. 28.17.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
one should [offer] five or seven Brahmins sesame seeds mixed with honey.
Whether they be black or otherwise,
let the King of Dharma be pleased— whatever dwells in your mind. 28.18–19.
Whatever evil has been committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment. 28,19.
Having fashioned a golden-naved [disc] from the skin of a black antelope, complete with its hooves,
and having covered it with sesame seeds, he who should give it away—
Hear now the fruit of his merit:
by him [is gained] a cave together with gold,
along with mountains, forests, and groves.
The earth is given with four faces; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having placed sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, 28.21–22.
"He who gives gold, the seeker of honey, to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds."
"One overcomes all evil deeds.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra. ||28||

29.2 One who practices celibacy becomes long-lived and handsome.
3. By practicing non-violence, one attains heaven.
29.3. 4. By entering the fire, one reaches the world of Brahmā. 29.4. 5. Through silence, one gains good fortune. 29.5.

6. He is the lord of the *nāgas* because he dwells in the water. 29,6. 7. He is free from disease, his treasury being exhausted. 29,7. 8. He is the giver of water, in whom all desires are fulfilled. 29,8.
9. One who gives food becomes clear-sighted and possessed of memory.
29.9. 10. One who gives protection from all dangers becomes wise. 29.10. 11.
By [giving] a vehicle yoked with oxen, one obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords. 29.11.
12. From the gift of beds and seats, one obtains lordship over the inner apartments. 29.12. 13. From the gift of an umbrella, one obtains a house. 29.13.
14. A giver of a house attains a city.
29.14. 15. A giver of shoes obtains a vehicle.
29.15. 16. Now they also cite this:
Whatever sin a man oppressed by his livelihood may commit,
it is [purified] even by [the gift of land] the size of a cow-hide.
One is purified by the gift of land. 29.16.
17 One should give a full water-pot to a Brahmin for the purpose of sipping water.
Having attained supreme satisfaction after passing away, the one born from Soma is born again as the equivalent of thousands of oxen. 29.17–18. [The merit of] thousands of oxen.
The gift of draft animals that carry heavy loads,
given according to the rules to a worthy recipient, is equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage. 29.18.
19. They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī; for these are indeed the most excellent among all gifts.
The gift of knowledge is superior to that;
it bestows the ultimate fruit and liberates one from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The wise person who, free from malice, follows this conduct with faith, being pure and self-controlled— 29.20.21— [attains the goal].
Whoever should uphold or even hear it,
having abandoned all evils,
shall be honored upon the surface of heaven.
"He is honored on the back of the firmament.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||29||
Practice righteousness, not unrighteousness; speak the truth, not falsehood.
Look upon the long, not the short; look upon the further shore, not this side. 30.1 The Brāhmaṇa becomes the fire. 30.2
For it is stated in the Śruti: "The Brahmin is indeed Agni.

5. In this regard, for the Brāhmaṇa, the sacrificial hall (*sadas*) is the body, the altar (*vedi*) is the resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the sacrifice is the self (*ātman*), the animal victim is the intellect (*buddhi*), the tethering rope is the seat (*sadas*), the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire, the navel is the *gārhapatya* fire, the stomach is the fire, the *adhvaryu* priest is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *hotṛ* priest is the in-breath (*apāna*), the *brahmā* priest is the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the *udgātṛ* priest is the levelled breath (*samāna*), the self and the senses are the sacrificial vessels. For one who knows thus, he offers the objects of the senses with the senses. This is also known in the *Kāṭhaka*: "He protects and saves the giver. 6. Moreover, they cite:
"It protects and saves the giver..."
And one's very self from sin,
by offering [oblations] into the fires of the Brahmins' mouths, which are well-fueled with the wood of the Vedas. 30.6.
That which does not spill over, does not cause distress, and does not cause one to commit transgression—
this is superior even to the Agnihotra sacrifice.
An oblation is poured into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. 30.7.
8 Meditation is the fire, truth the piling of the altar, patience the offering, modesty the sacrificial ladle, non-violence the sacrificial cake, and contentment the [priest].
The wise man, considering that the sacrificial post is a hardship for living beings and that the gift of fearlessness is the true sacrificial fee, brings his ritual to an end within his own mind.
(30.8) As one ages, the hair grows old. (30.9)
The teeth decay as one decays; but the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay even as one decays. 30.9.
That which is difficult for the foolish to abandon,
which does not decay even as one decays,
is that disease which ends with life itself.
"Happiness belongs to one who abandons that craving.
(30.10) "Adoration be to Vasiṣṭha, the son of Urvaśī, born of Mitra and Varuṇa, the one of a hundred sacrifices—to Vasiṣṭha, to Vasiṣṭha! (30.11)
